Its dating has been contested from both directions, with Janet Abu-Lughod arguing in Before European Hegemony that a thirteenth-century Eurasian world system already linked Bruges to Guangzhou through eight overlapping circuits, and Frank later arguing in ReORIENT that Asia remained the world economy's centre of gravity until about 1800, with Europe a latecomer using American silver to buy its way into Asian trade.

The permanent contribution is the discipline of relational thinking. It is a standing warning that comparing two societies as though they were independent specimens can be badly misleading when one has been shaping the other for centuries. The plantation complex of the Caribbean, the cotton fields of the American South and the mills of Lancashire were not three separate economies that happened to trade; they were one production system distributed across three continents, and the profits, the labour regime and the technology are unintelligible apart from each other.

sections.heading: The Logic of Comparison: Mill's Methods and Their Limits
sections.body:
The comparative approach borrows its formal skeleton from John Stuart Mill, whose System of Logic of 1843 set out canons of induction that historians still use, usually without naming them. Two matter most. The method of agreement examines cases that share an outcome and looks for the one antecedent they all share: if industrial breakthroughs occurred in Britain, Belgium and the American Northeast, and all three had abundant accessible coal, coal becomes a candidate cause. The method of difference examines cases that are alike in most respects but differ in the outcome, and looks for the antecedent that differs: this is the more powerful of the two, because it approximates a controlled experiment.

Comparativists formalised these as the most-similar and most-different systems designs. The most-similar design takes cases that resemble one another closely — two Chinese provinces, France and Germany in 1900 — so that shared features can be treated as held constant, and attention falls on the few differences. The most-different design takes cases with almost nothing in common and asks what the handful of shared elements might explain; if peasant revolt occurs in eighteenth-century France, nineteenth-century Russia and twentieth-century China, whatever those three share is a strong candidate.

The trouble is that Mill's canons were designed for closed systems with few variables and many cases, and history offers open systems with very many variables and very few cases. Three specific problems follow. The first is the small-N problem: with five cases and twenty plausible causes, the data cannot in principle discriminate between competing explanations, a limitation formalised as the many-variables, small-N problem. The second is equifinality: the same outcome may be reached by different routes, so finding a shared antecedent does not establish that it was necessary. The third is interaction: causes in history rarely act singly, and a factor may be decisive only in the presence of another, which the canons handle poorly.

Historians have developed partial remedies. Process tracing examines the intervening steps within a case to check whether the proposed mechanism actually operated, rather than resting on correlation across cases; if coal caused industrialisation, one should be able to observe the specific channels — falling fuel prices, the substitution of steam for water power, particular firms making particular decisions. Counterfactual reasoning, used disciplined and minimally, asks what would plausibly have followed had one antecedent been absent, changing as little else as possible. Neither is a substitute for evidence, but both convert a loose analogy into a testable claim.

A third remedy, developed by Charles Ragin from the late 1980s, is qualitative comparative analysis, which uses Boolean algebra to identify which combinations of conditions are consistently associated with an outcome across a modest number of cases. Its value is that it takes seriously what Mill's canons handle badly: causes usually work in packages, and several different packages may each be sufficient. Its limitation is that the analyst still decides which conditions enter the model and where thresholds fall, so judgement is relocated rather than removed. As a discipline for making assumptions visible it helps; as an answer machine it does not.

sections.heading: Choosing Units, and Galton's Problem
sections.body:
Every comparison begins with a decision that is often made unconsciously and frequently determines the answer: what is being compared with what. The choice of unit is not neutral. Comparing "Europe" with "China" appears symmetrical but is not — one is a continent of competing states with a combined population comparable to China's, the other a single political entity. If the question concerns political fragmentation, that asymmetry is the whole point; if it concerns economic performance, comparing all of Europe with all of China averages together the Yangzi delta with Gansu and Lancashire with Calabria, and averages can hide the very divergence being investigated.

Kenneth Pomeranz addressed this directly in The Great Divergence of 2000 by insisting on comparing like with like: the Yangzi delta against England and the Netherlands, not China against Europe. Comparing regions of similar population, commercialisation and land quality removes an enormous amount of noise. The general principle is that units should be chosen so that the features held constant genuinely are constant, and the unit should be defined by the question rather than inherited from modern political maps.

The second structural hazard carries a name from anthropology. In 1889 Edward Tylor presented a paper correlating marriage customs across many societies, and Francis Galton objected that the societies were not independent: if two peoples share a custom because one learned it from the other or both inherited it from a common ancestor, then counting them as two confirmations of a correlation is double counting. This is Galton's problem, and it is pervasive in world history. If parliamentary institutions appear in fifteen countries, that is not fifteen independent instances of institutional evolution; it is a smaller number of origins plus diffusion, imposition and imitation. Treating diffused traits as independent evidence systematically inflates confidence.

There is no complete solution, but there are honest practices. Establish the historical relationship between cases before comparing them: were they in contact, did one conquer or colonise the other, did both draw on a shared predecessor. Where cases are connected, say so and shift the question from "why did both develop X" to "why was X adopted here and refused there", which is often more revealing. Where possible, seek genuinely independent cases: the separate inventions of agriculture in Southwest Asia, China, Mesoamerica, the Andes, New Guinea and eastern North America are close to independent trials and therefore unusually informative. And be explicit about the level of aggregation, because comparisons that hold at the level of empires often reverse at the level of provinces.

That last point has a formal name borrowed from geography: the modifiable areal unit problem. Relationships between two variables can change in magnitude and even in sign depending on how the map is cut into units, and history is exposed to this because its units are inherited rather than designed. Averaging Britain's real wages with Ireland's can turn a sharp internal divergence into a flat national mean. Whenever a comparison is made at one level, ask what it would look like one level down, and trust a result that survives both far more than one that does not.

sections.heading: Scales of Analysis: From the Village to Deep Time
sections.body:
World history is not committed to a single scale, and choosing one is an analytical decision with consequences. At the largest end sits big history, associated with David Christian and taught since the late 1980s, which begins at the Big Bang roughly 13.8 billion years ago and treats human history as the latest phase in a sequence of rising complexity: stars, chemical elements, planets, life, brains, language, agriculture, industry. Its organising concept is the "Goldilocks condition" — the narrow range of energy flows and material conditions that permits each new level of complexity — and its unifying measure is energy density. This scale is excellent for placing humans in a physical context and for showing that agriculture and industry were transformations of energy capture, and poor for anything requiring the granularity of individual agency.

Below that sits deep human history, running from the emergence of anatomically modern humans some 300,000 years ago through the peopling of Australia by about 65,000 years ago and the Americas by at least 15,000 years ago. This scale has been transformed since 2010 by ancient DNA, which has resolved questions written sources never could: the interbreeding of modern humans with Neanderthals leaving roughly one to two per cent Neanderthal ancestry in people outside Africa, the steppe migration associated with the Yamnaya that reshaped European ancestry after about 3000 BCE.

The conventional macro scale of world history runs from agriculture to the present, roughly 12,000 years, and is where most comparison happens: states, empires, trade circuits, religions, epidemics. Below it lies the meso scale of regions and networks — the Indian Ocean monsoon system, the Saharan caravan routes, the Baltic grain trade — which often makes better analytical sense than either continents or countries.

The smallest scale still counts as world history when the local case is used to illuminate global processes. Microhistory, developed by Carlo Ginzburg and Giovanni Levi in the 1970s, takes a single village, trial or life and reads it intensively. Global microhistory applies the same technique to a person who crossed worlds — a captured slave, a Jesuit in Beijing, a Gujarati merchant in Aden — using the individual case as a probe that reveals how large structures actually operated in practice.

The essential discipline is to know what each scale can show and what it necessarily hides. Aggregate scales reveal structure and conceal agency; fine scales reveal contingency and cannot establish generality. A strong world-historical argument usually moves deliberately between at least two, using the large scale to establish the pattern and the small scale to demonstrate the mechanism that produced it.

A practical warning about scale applies to readers as much as writers. The larger the scale, the greater the compression, and compression is not neutral: it preserves what recurs and deletes what happened once. At ten thousand years the Mongol conquests are a paragraph and a single life is invisible — appropriate for questions about energy and population, disastrous for questions about how power was exercised. A history written entirely at one scale is partial, and the partiality is systematic rather than random.

sections.heading: Comparison Versus Connection: Two Ways to Be Global
sections.body:
There are two distinct ways to make history global, and confusing them causes a great deal of muddle. The comparative move treats societies as separate cases and asks how they differed and why. The connective move treats them as parts of one field and asks how they influenced each other. Both are legitimate; they answer different questions and require different evidence.

Connective history has produced some of the field's most durable results. Alfred Crosby's The Columbian Exchange of 1972 traced the biological consequences of 1492 in both directions: American crops raising carrying capacity across Afro-Eurasia, with maize and cassava supporting population growth in Africa and the potato transforming northern European diets, while Old World pathogens — smallpox above all, with measles, typhus and influenza — devastated American populations that had no acquired immunity, in a collapse most estimates put between fifty and ninety per cent over the first century and a half. Philip Curtin's work on trade diaspora, Janet Abu-Lughod's on the thirteenth-century circuits, and the large literature on the Indian Ocean all belong to this tradition.

Historians have developed vocabulary for finer distinctions. Transfer history studies what moves and how it is transformed in transit — a doctrine, a technology, a legal form rarely arrives unchanged. Entangled history, or histoire croisée as formulated by Michael Werner and Bénédicte Zimmermann in the early 2000s, insists that the entities being compared were often partly constituted by their interaction, so that treating them as independent is a fiction: modern "Europe" and modern "India" were each partly made by their encounter. Connected histories, in Sanjay Subrahmanyam's formulation from 1997, argue that early modern Eurasia should be read as a single arena in which millenarian expectations, gunpowder empires and travelling ideas circulated across supposed civilisational boundaries.

The relationship between the two moves is not opposition but sequence. Comparison without attention to connection produces the Galton error of counting borrowed traits as independent evidence. Connection without comparison produces narratives of flow that cannot explain why the same thing arriving in two places had different effects — gunpowder reached Japan and Java in the sixteenth century and did very different work in each. The strongest practice establishes the connections first, so that they become part of the explanation rather than a hidden contaminant, and then compares the differential responses. The question shifts from "why are these two different" to "why did these two, exposed to much the same thing, respond differently", which is both more answerable and more interesting.

The gunpowder example repays a little detail, because it shows what the combined method can do. Firearms reached Japan in 1543 through Portuguese traders at Tanegashima; within decades Japanese smiths were producing matchlocks in quantity, and by the battle of Nagashino in 1575 volley fire was decisive. Yet after the Tokugawa consolidation the technology was deliberately constrained, and its military prominence declined for two centuries. In Europe the same weapon drove a sustained arms race in fortification, drill and state finance. The input was identical; the outcomes diverged because the political settlements differed. Neither pure comparison nor pure connection could have shown that.

sections.heading: A Worked Case: The Great Divergence Debate
sections.body:
The debate over why sustained industrial growth began in northwestern Europe is the best available demonstration of comparative method under strain, because it has been argued at length by serious people using largely the same evidence to reach incompatible conclusions.

The older answer, dominant into the 1980s, located European advantage far back: in Roman law, Christian rationality, feudal contract, the competitive state system, or the scientific revolution. Europe was held to have been pulling ahead since 1500 or earlier. David Landes in The Wealth and Poverty of Nations of 1998 gave a late and forceful version, emphasising culture, work discipline and openness to innovation.

The revisionist case, made most influentially by Kenneth Pomeranz in 2000 and supported by work from Bin Wong, Jack Goldstone and others, argued that as late as 1750 the most advanced regions of Europe and Asia were roughly comparable on measurable dimensions: life expectancy, calorie intake, market integration measured by grain price convergence, female labour-force participation, agricultural productivity per acre, and rates of proto-industrial activity. On this reading, the divergence is late and abrupt, opening decisively only after about 1800. Pomeranz's explanation is not a European virtue but two contingent relaxations of an ecological constraint that both regions faced. First, Britain's coal lay near the surface, near water transport and near the manufacturing centres — Chinese coal was concentrated in the northwest, far from the Yangzi delta, a transport problem that is a fact about geology rather than culture. Second, the Americas supplied Britain with "ghost acreage": by one estimate the cotton, sugar and timber imported around 1830 would have required something on the order of ten to twenty million acres of British land to replace, land Britain did not have.

The critics responded on evidence and on logic. Robert Allen argued that British wages were unusually high relative to energy costs, making labour-saving machinery profitable there and unprofitable elsewhere — a price-ratio explanation that keeps the mechanism economic while restoring an internal European cause. Others, including Stephen Broadberry and Bishnupriya Gupta, produced wage and price series suggesting the gap in real incomes opened earlier than Pomeranz allowed, perhaps from the seventeenth century. Joel Mokyr emphasised the Industrial Enlightenment: the specific institutions linking artisan practice to natural philosophy.

The debate remains genuinely unresolved, and that is the point worth taking. Its methodological legacy is nonetheless firm: comparisons must be region to region rather than continent to continent, the burden of proof lies on claims of early European exceptionalism, and quantitative series must be interrogated for how their underlying baskets and deflators were constructed before their conclusions are accepted.

It is also a useful case for seeing how a good comparative argument accumulates value even when it loses. Whether or not Pomeranz was right about 1750, the debate forced the construction of Chinese, Indian and Ottoman wage and price series that had never existed, established the Yangzi delta as a serious economic region, and retired a family of explanations resting on supposed Asian despotism. Arguments in history are often productive this way: the contest generates evidence that outlives whichever side commissioned it.

sections.heading: Sources and the Problem of Asymmetric Archives
sections.body:
A comparison is only as good as the evidence on both sides, and evidence about the past is distributed with brutal unevenness. Some societies produced enormous quantities of writing on durable material and preserved it in institutions that survived; others wrote on palm leaf and bark in humid climates, or recorded obligations in knotted cords, or transmitted knowledge orally. The result is that the archive is not a sample of the past but a residue shaped by what was written, what survived, what was collected and what has been catalogued and translated.

The consequences for comparison are severe and systematic. If Chinese local gazetteers record grain prices for hundreds of counties across five centuries while comparable West African data do not exist, then any comparison of price volatility will find the Chinese case legible and the African case blank — and the naive reading of a blank is absence rather than silence. Colonial archives compound the problem: for much of Africa, South Asia and the Pacific, the densest documentation of the nineteenth century was produced by administrations with specific interests in categorising, taxing and controlling, so the categories embedded in the data are the colonisers' categories.

Historians manage this in several ways. The first is triangulation with non-written evidence. Archaeology supplies settlement size, house floor area, diet from isotopes, and trade from ceramic and metal sourcing, and it is available for societies with no writing at all. Skeletal evidence gives stature, which is a reasonable proxy for childhood nutrition and can be compared across regions. Palaeoclimate archives — ice cores, tree rings, speleothems, lake sediments — supply an independently dated environmental record. Historical linguistics reconstructs contact and migration from loanwords and sound changes. Genetics supplies population movement directly.

The second is oral tradition treated critically. Jan Vansina's work from the 1960s onward established methods for using oral tradition as historical evidence: attend to genre, since a king list and a praise poem have different relations to fact; collect multiple independent versions; look for the structural features of transmission that distort, such as telescoping of the middle past and the tendency of genealogies to be adjusted to serve present claims.

The third is honesty about asymmetry. When one side of a comparison rests on tax registers and the other on three travellers' accounts, the appropriate conclusion is often that the comparison cannot be made at the precision desired. Stating that plainly is better scholarship than manufacturing a number. A useful habit is to write down, for each case, what kind of evidence supports each claim and how it could be wrong, before drawing the comparison — an error budget for history. Doing this before rather than after the argument is formed matters, because the temptation to grade the evidence by whether it agrees with you is powerful and largely unconscious.

sections.heading: Counting the Past: Quantitative World History and Its Uncertainties
sections.body:
Much of modern world history rests on numbers: populations, real wages, urbanisation rates, energy consumption, book production, ship tonnage. Quantification permits comparison across societies whose qualitative descriptions are incommensurable, and it disciplines argument by making claims falsifiable. It also carries risks that are frequently understated, and a reader should know how these series are built.

Population series before the nineteenth century are almost entirely reconstructions. Angus Maddison's widely used estimates of population and GDP back to year 1 CE are best understood as informed conjecture: for many regions and periods they are extrapolations from a small number of anchor points, and their apparent precision is an artefact of arithmetic rather than of evidence. When such a series says world population was 268 million in the year 1000, the honest reading is a wide band, not a figure. The same applies to Americas population in 1491, where scholarly estimates range from about 40 million to over 100 million, a spread that changes the interpretation of post-contact collapse enormously.

Real wage series, the workhorse of the Great Divergence debate, are built by dividing a money wage by the cost of a defined basket of goods. Every step is contestable: which occupations, whether the wage is daily or annual, how many days a year were worked, what goes in the basket, and how to handle goods present in one society and absent in another. Robert Allen's "bare bones" and "respectability" baskets were designed to be comparable across Eurasia, but the choice of basket alone can move the measured gap between London and Beijing substantially.

Energy accounting is more robust because the physics is fixed. Comparing societies by energy capture per capita per year — from food, fodder, fuel and later fossil sources — gives a genuinely cross-cultural measure, and Ian Morris used a version of it in his index of social development, alongside urbanisation, information technology and war-making capacity. Even here the coefficients are judgement calls, and Morris was explicit that his index is a heuristic.

The working rules are straightforward. Ask what the underlying observations are, not just what the table says. Prefer ratios and trends over levels, since systematic biases often cancel in a ratio. Present ranges rather than point estimates for anything reconstructed. And treat any series whose error bars are never displayed with suspicion, because the absence of stated uncertainty is usually a sign that it was never calculated.

There is a further hazard specific to long series, sometimes called the tyranny of the available number. Once a figure is published it gets cited, then cited from the citation, and after a few rounds its original basis is no longer visible to anyone using it. Maddison's tables acquired exactly this status. The remedy is not to abandon quantification, which remains the best defence against argument by anecdote, but to trace at least one number in any series back to its source before building on it. Doing so is usually sobering and occasionally decisive: more than one confident claim about pre-modern living standards rests on a single tax document read in one particular way.

sections.heading: Environment, Disease, and Ecology as Comparative Frames
sections.body:
One of the most productive shifts in world history has been to treat the natural world as an active participant rather than a stage. This produced a set of comparative frames that cut across cultural boundaries, because climate, pathogens and soils operate on all societies by the same rules.

The disease frame is the most developed. William McNeill's Plagues and Peoples of 1976 argued that each large agrarian civilisation developed its own pool of endemic infections to which its population acquired partial immunity, and that when previously separated pools met, the result was catastrophic mortality on the side lacking exposure. This explains the asymmetry of 1492 without recourse to any claim about the peoples involved: Eurasian populations, living densely alongside domesticated cattle, pigs and poultry, had accumulated a battery of zoonotic diseases; American populations, with few domesticable herd animals, had not. The mechanism is ecological.

The climate frame has strengthened enormously as palaeoclimate data have improved. There is now a well-dated record from ice cores, tree rings and cave deposits allowing environmental events to be compared against historical records worldwide. The eruption of Samalas in Indonesia in 1257, one of the largest of the last several thousand years, appears in ice cores in both hemispheres and coincides with documented famine. The cluster of eruptions beginning in 536 CE produced the coldest decade in some 2,000 years of tree-ring reconstruction, with dust veils recorded in Byzantine and Chinese sources. The Little Ice Age, a period of cooling roughly from the fourteenth to the nineteenth centuries, has been proposed by Geoffrey Parker as a contributing cause of the seventeenth-century crisis of wars and revolutions from Britain to China.

Caution is essential here, because environmental explanation slides easily into determinism. The correct form of the argument is that environmental shocks alter the constraints and the probabilities, and that the outcome depends on social capacity: whether granaries existed, whether relief could be moved, whether legitimacy survived. Two societies hit by the same drought can diverge entirely. Jared Diamond's Guns, Germs, and Steel of 1997 made the most-read environmental argument — that the east–west axis of Eurasia allowed crops and animals to spread along constant latitudes while Africa's and the Americas' north–south axes did not — and drew heavy criticism precisely for compressing the space in which human choices operate. The frame is valuable; the determinism is not.

The soil and water frame is less famous and often more useful at the regional scale. Irrigation societies face common problems — silting, salinisation, coordinating maintenance labour, allocating water between upstream and downstream users — recurring from Mesopotamia to the Nile to the Indus. Salinisation in southern Mesopotamia, visible in the cuneiform record's shift from wheat toward salt-tolerant barley across the third and second millennia BCE, shows how a productive technique can degrade its own basis over centuries. Karl Wittfogel's claim that large irrigation works necessarily produced despotic states has not survived, since many were managed locally, but the observation that shared water forces shared institutions has held up well.

sections.heading: Periodisation: Cutting Time Without Cheating
sections.body:
Any world history must divide time into periods, and every division is an argument disguised as a convenience. The familiar tripartite scheme of ancient, medieval and modern was devised by Italian humanists to describe their own situation: a classical antiquity they admired, a middle age they despised, and a rebirth they were living. Applied globally it produces nonsense — there is no useful sense in which Song China or Mali under Mansa Musa was living in the "middle" of anything — yet it survives in curricula and library classifications and quietly shapes what gets compared with what.

World historians have proposed alternatives, each with its own logic. One approach periodises by the extent of interaction: an era of separate regional worlds, an era of hemispheric networks after roughly 500 BCE, a genuinely global era after 1492 when the Americas and Pacific were linked, and an accelerated era after about 1850 with steamships, telegraphs and mass migration. This has the virtue of being defined by the field's own subject matter, connection, rather than borrowed from one region's politics.

Another periodises by energy regime: foraging, agrarian, and fossil-fuel societies, with the transition to agriculture beginning about 10,000 BCE in several places independently and the fossil transition beginning in the eighteenth century. This is defensible on physical grounds and correlates with population, urbanisation and inequality, but it flattens three millennia of agrarian variation into one long stretch.

A third uses political-economic markers: the axial age proposed by Karl Jaspers for the middle of the first millennium BCE, when Confucian, Buddhist, Hebrew prophetic, Zoroastrian and Greek philosophical traditions appeared in a comparatively short window across Eurasia; the early modern period from roughly 1450 to 1800 defined by gunpowder empires, silver flows and maritime linkage; the modern from the double revolution of industry and political mass mobilisation.

Certain hazards recur. Periodising by European events — dating "early modern" from 1492 or 1453 — imports a Eurocentric frame through the back door. Periodising by a single criterion hides the fact that different processes have different rhythms, so that political, economic, demographic and intellectual periodisations do not coincide. And sharp boundaries misrepresent transitions that took generations.

The workable discipline is to state the criterion explicitly, to allow different periodisations for different questions rather than insisting on one master scheme, and to remember Braudel's point that the layers move at different speeds. A date is a claim about what mattered; it should be defended, not assumed.

One further complication deserves mention, because it is now unavoidable. The proposal to name a geological epoch the Anthropocene, marking the point at which human activity became the dominant force shaping the earth system, is simultaneously a periodisation question. Candidate start dates carry different arguments: around 1610, when the collapse of American populations allowed forest regrowth and a measurable dip in atmospheric carbon dioxide; the late eighteenth century with fossil fuel; or the mid-twentieth-century Great Acceleration, with radionuclides from nuclear testing as a sharp global marker. Whichever is chosen, the effect is to make world history and earth history share a timeline, which is a genuinely new situation for the discipline.

sections.heading: Failure Modes: How Comparative Arguments Go Wrong
sections.body:
Comparative world history fails in recognisable ways, and knowing the catalogue is the best protection against repeating it.

Teleology is the most common. This is reading the past as an approach march toward a known present, so that whatever led to the outcome is treated as significant and whatever did not is dismissed as a dead end. It makes every historical actor a rehearsal for someone later. The corrective is to reconstruct the situation as it appeared to contemporaries, with the alternatives that were genuinely open, and to take seriously the paths that were not taken.

Anachronism is the projection of modern categories onto societies that lacked them. Applying "economy", "religion", "state" or "race" to periods where those domains were not separated distorts what is being compared. Medieval Christian Europe did not have a religion in the sense of one option among several; the term as used today emerged from early modern European experience.

Cherry-picking is selecting the cases that support the thesis. If a claim about the effects of political fragmentation rests on Europe and classical Greece while ignoring the Warring States, Renaissance Italy's outcomes and post-colonial Africa, the sample was chosen by the conclusion. The remedy is to define the case universe before selecting: state the criteria for inclusion, then take all cases meeting them.

Selection on the dependent variable is a related and subtler error: examining only cases where the outcome occurred. Studying ten successful revolutions establishes nothing about the causes of revolution without the cases where the same conditions produced no revolution.

Reification treats the comparative units as real, bounded things. "The West", "Islam", "China" are analytical conveniences that dissolve on inspection into diversity and change, and arguments that attribute agency or character to them are usually attributing it to something that does not exist in that form.

Determinism, whether geographic, cultural or economic, removes the space in which the causes actually operate. Presenting a factor as decisive without showing the mechanism connecting it to the outcome, and without the cases where the same factor produced a different result, is assertion.

Finally, essentialised culture as explanation — attributing divergent outcomes to a supposedly stable national or civilisational character — has an especially poor record. The same "Confucian culture" was cited to explain Chinese stagnation before 1980 and East Asian dynamism afterwards. When an explanation can accommodate opposite outcomes, it explains neither.

Two smaller errors round out the list. Presentism uses the past as a supply depot for present arguments, selecting whatever supports a current position and treating the rest as noise; the symptom is a history whose conclusions were available before the research began. And the asymmetry of explanation is the habit of explaining the unfamiliar case while leaving the familiar one unexplained — asking why China did not industrialise while treating British industrialisation as needing no account. Both cases require explanation, and the discipline of writing the question in symmetrical form, so that each side is equally strange, catches a surprising amount.

sections.heading: Doing It: A Working Method for a Comparative Study
sections.body: Comparative world history can be practised deliberately rather than intuitively, and a repeatable sequence helps. The following procedure suits a study of any size, from an essay to a book, and its value lies chiefly in forcing decisions to be made explicitly and recorded before the evidence is fitted to them.
steps: State the puzzle as a contrast, not a description. Write one sentence of the form 'X occurred in A but not in B, although both had C, D and E.' A comparison without a puzzle produces a catalogue rather than an argument, and writing the sentence exposes immediately whether the shared conditions are real.

Define the case universe before choosing cases. Write down the criteria for inclusion — a population range, a date window, a defining institution — and then list every case meeting them, including the inconvenient ones. Selecting cases after knowing their outcomes is the single most common way a comparative argument becomes unfalsifiable.

Choose the unit of comparison so that the things you intend to hold constant genuinely are constant. Prefer regions of comparable population, climate and commercialisation over continents or modern states; if you compare England with the Yangzi delta rather than Europe with China, say why in a sentence the reader can evaluate.

Map the connections between cases before comparing them. Ask whether one conquered, colonised, traded with, converted or copied the other, and whether both drew on a shared predecessor. Where connection exists, reformulate the question as differential response — why the same input produced different outputs — rather than pretending independence.

Build a matched evidence base. For each case, record what kind of source supports each key claim, its date, who produced it and for what purpose. Where the evidence is asymmetric — tax registers on one side, travellers' reports on the other — write down the asymmetry and set the precision of the comparison accordingly.

Specify the candidate causes as mechanisms, not labels. 'Culture' and 'institutions' are not mechanisms; 'partible inheritance fragmented holdings below the threshold for plough teams within three generations' is. Each candidate should imply observable intermediate steps.

Test each mechanism inside a single case by process tracing. Look for the intervening evidence the mechanism predicts, and equally for evidence it forbids. A mechanism that survives this within one case has earned the right to be tested across cases.

Run the cross-case comparison with the most-similar and most-different designs deliberately, and state which you are using. Note explicitly any candidate cause that varies with the outcome only because the cases are not independent.
Construct the disconfirming test. Name in advance the evidence that would show your explanation wrong, then go and look for it. If no such evidence is conceivable, the argument is not yet historical.

Write the uncertainty into the conclusion. Distinguish what the evidence establishes, what it makes probable, and what remains conjecture, and give the strongest surviving rival explanation a fair statement rather than a caricature.

guides.title: Big History: From the Big Bang to the Present
guides.summary: A single connected account of the past 13.8 billion years, from the Big Bang through the formation of stars, elements, planets and life to agriculture, cities and the industrial world, organised around the thresholds at which genuinely new kinds of complexity appeared and the energy flows that sustain them.

sections.heading: What Big History Is and Why Scale Changes the Story
sections.body:
Big History is the attempt to tell the whole past as one connected narrative, beginning at the origin of the universe and ending in the present, using the findings of cosmology, geology, chemistry, biology, archaeology and conventional history as chapters of a single account rather than as separate disciplines. The name and the modern academic form are associated above all with the historian David Christian, who began teaching such a course at Macquarie University in Sydney in 1989 and set out its framework in his 2004 book Maps of Time. The approach spread through the International Big History Association, founded in 2010, and through the Big History Project, a free online curriculum funded from 2011 by Bill Gates after he encountered Christian's lectures.

The intellectual justification is that the conventional boundary of history, drawn where written records begin about 5,000 years ago, is an accident of evidence rather than a real division in the past. It survives because historians were trained to read documents while the deeper past belonged to scientists reading rocks, fossils and starlight. Over the twentieth century that division became untenable, because a whole family of new dating techniques gave the pre-literate past a firm chronology for the first time. Radiometric dating, developed after Ernest Rutherford's suggestion in 1904 and made practical by Arthur Holmes, gave the Earth an age. Radiocarbon dating, devised by Willard Libby in 1949, dated the human past. Hubble's 1929 observation that distant galaxies recede faster the further away they are gave the universe an age. For the first time it became possible to place every kind of event on one absolute timescale, which is the precondition for telling one story.

Big History is usually organised around thresholds, moments when something genuinely new appeared that had not existed before and could not easily have been predicted from what came earlier. Christian's standard list has eight: the Big Bang itself, the first stars, the manufacture of the chemical elements, the formation of planetary systems including Earth, the origin of life, the emergence of humans with collective learning, the appearance of agriculture, and the modern revolution of the last few centuries. Each threshold requires particular circumstances, often called Goldilocks conditions after the porridge that was neither too hot nor too cold, and each produces structures more complex, more energy-hungry and more fragile than what preceded it.

The framework carries its own hazards, and honest practitioners name them. Telling one story invites the illusion that the past was aimed at us, which is a mistake: complexity is rare, local and reversible, and the universe as a whole is running steadily toward disorder. Compressing millennia into paragraphs also flattens the particular, and much of the human past resists it. The value of the scale is not that it replaces detailed history but that it supplies the context detailed history normally leaves out.

sections.heading: The Big Bang and the First Second
sections.body:
The universe began, so far as physics can currently reach, about 13.8 billion years ago. The most precise figure comes from the European Space Agency's Planck satellite, which in 2018 reported 13.797 billion years with an uncertainty of about 23 million years, derived from the detailed pattern of temperature ripples in the oldest light in the sky. There is a genuine and unresolved tension in cosmology here, since measurements of the present expansion rate made using nearby supernovae give a slightly different value from those derived from the early universe, a discrepancy known as the Hubble tension that has resisted explanation for over a decade.

The phrase Big Bang misleads twice over. It was not an explosion into pre-existing space, since space itself was part of what expanded, and there was no centre from which it happened; every point in the universe is equally the centre of its own expanding view. Nor does the theory describe an origin from nothing. It describes what happened to an extremely hot, extremely dense state as it expanded and cooled. What preceded that state, or whether the question is even meaningful, is not known.

The earliest instants are reconstructed by running the known laws backwards, and confidence falls sharply the further back one goes. Before about 10 to the minus 43 seconds, the Planck time, gravity would have been strong enough at quantum scales that general relativity and quantum mechanics both apply and no one has a theory that combines them; this interval is genuinely beyond current physics. Between roughly 10 to the minus 36 and 10 to the minus 32 seconds, most cosmologists accept that the universe underwent inflation, an episode proposed by Alan Guth in 1980 in which space expanded by a factor of at least 10 to the 26 in a fraction of an instant. Inflation is favoured because it neatly explains why the universe looks the same in all directions, why space is so nearly flat, and why the density ripples that later became galaxies have exactly the statistical character observed. It remains a well-supported framework rather than a proven event.

As expansion cooled the universe, the four forces separated out from what may have been a single unified interaction, and matter condensed from energy through the relation between the two that Einstein published in 1905. A crucial and unexplained asymmetry appeared: for roughly every billion antimatter particles there were a billion and one particles of matter. Almost everything annihilated, and the tiny surplus is all the matter that exists. By one microsecond the universe had cooled to about 10 trillion degrees, and quarks could bind into protons and neutrons. Had the surplus of matter over antimatter been exactly zero, the universe would today contain radiation and nothing else; why it was not zero is an open question, and the search for the responsible asymmetry in particle physics has so far come up short by several orders of magnitude.

sections.heading: Making the First Atoms and the Oldest Light
sections.body:
Between roughly ten seconds and twenty minutes after the beginning, the universe passed through a window in which it was cool enough for atomic nuclei to hold together but still hot and dense enough for fusion to occur. This episode, Big Bang nucleosynthesis, manufactured the lightest elements and then shut down as expansion dropped the temperature below the threshold for fusion. It produced a universe consisting by mass of about 75 per cent hydrogen and 25 per cent helium-4, with traces of deuterium, helium-3 and lithium-7, and essentially nothing heavier. Carbon, oxygen, iron and everything else the world is made of did not exist yet.

The observational check on this is one of the strongest results in cosmology. The predicted abundances depend sensitively on the density of ordinary matter, and measurements of primordial deuterium in distant gas clouds agree with the value derived independently from the cosmic microwave background to within a few per cent. Lithium-7 is the exception: the observed abundance in ancient stars is roughly three times lower than predicted, a discrepancy known as the lithium problem that has been argued over since the 1980s and is still unresolved.

For the next 380,000 years the universe was an opaque plasma of bare nuclei and free electrons. Light could not travel far without scattering off an electron, exactly as it cannot travel far through fog. Then expansion brought the temperature down to about 3,000 kelvin, cool enough for electrons to be captured into orbit around nuclei to form neutral atoms, an event confusingly called recombination although nothing had combined before. Space abruptly became transparent, and the light released at that moment has been travelling ever since.

That light is the cosmic microwave background, discovered accidentally in 1964 by Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson at Bell Labs, who found a persistent hiss in a horn antenna that they could not remove and initially blamed on pigeon droppings. Stretched by 13.8 billion years of cosmic expansion, its temperature has fallen from 3,000 kelvin to 2.725 kelvin, placing it in the microwave band. It is astonishingly uniform, the same in every direction to about one part in 100,000, and those faint variations are the seeds of everything. Regions very slightly denser than average pulled in matter gravitationally, grew denser still, and eventually collapsed into the first structures.

Mapping those ripples with the COBE satellite in 1992, WMAP from 2001 and Planck from 2009 is how the age, geometry and composition of the universe were pinned down. The composition is humbling: roughly 5 per cent ordinary atomic matter, about 27 per cent dark matter whose gravity is detected but whose nature is unknown, and about 68 per cent dark energy driving accelerating expansion, discovered in 1998 and still unexplained.

sections.heading: The First Stars and the Architecture of Galaxies
sections.body:
After recombination the universe entered what astronomers call the cosmic dark ages, a stretch of perhaps a hundred million years containing no light source at all: only expanding, cooling, neutral hydrogen and helium, and the invisible scaffolding of dark matter. Nothing shone, but gravity was working. Dark matter, unable to radiate away energy and therefore unable to collapse into small dense objects, gathered instead into vast diffuse haloes, and ordinary gas fell into the gravitational wells those haloes had already dug. This is why dark matter matters to the story: without it, structure would have formed far more slowly, and the universe would look nothing like the one observed.

Where gas accumulated densely enough, it collapsed under its own weight. Compressing a gas heats it, and if the heat cannot escape the rising pressure halts the collapse. Early clouds could shed heat only feebly, through molecular hydrogen, which is a poor coolant, so they had to grow very massive before collapse could run away. The first stars, called Population III, are therefore thought to have been monsters, perhaps tens to hundreds of times the mass of the Sun, blazing blue-white and burning out in only a few million years. None has ever been observed directly; their existence is a robust theoretical inference, and finding one, or its chemical fingerprint, is a major goal of the James Webb Space Telescope, launched in December 2021.

Star formation crosses its own threshold when the core of a collapsing cloud reaches roughly 10 million kelvin. At that temperature hydrogen nuclei, ordinarily repelled by their mutual positive charge, collide hard enough that quantum tunnelling lets them fuse into helium. Fusion releases energy because the helium nucleus weighs slightly less than the four protons that made it, the missing mass appearing as energy. That outward pressure balances gravity's inward pull, and the star settles into a stable configuration that can last from a few million years for the largest to trillions for the smallest.

The first stars ended violently, and their deaths lit and enriched the universe. Their intense ultraviolet output stripped electrons from the surrounding hydrogen again in a process called reionisation, largely complete by about a billion years after the beginning. Their explosions scattered the first heavy elements into space, so that later generations of stars formed from gas already seasoned with carbon and oxygen.

Meanwhile gravity organised matter on the largest scales. Stars gathered into galaxies of a hundred million to a trillion stars, galaxies into groups and clusters, and clusters into filaments and sheets surrounding vast near-empty voids, a cosmic web tens of millions of light years across. The Milky Way, an ordinary barred spiral containing perhaps 100 to 400 billion stars, took shape early and has grown by swallowing smaller galaxies ever since.

sections.heading: Stellar Nucleosynthesis: Where the Elements Came From
sections.body:
Every atom in a human body heavier than hydrogen was manufactured inside a star or in a stellar explosion. This is not a metaphor. The calcium in bone, the iron in blood, the carbon in every protein and the oxygen in every breath were assembled by nuclear fusion in objects that no longer exist, then blown into space, mixed into a cloud of gas, and incorporated into the Earth. The insight was worked out in a landmark 1957 paper by Margaret Burbidge, Geoffrey Burbidge, William Fowler and Fred Hoyle, still known simply as B2FH, and it is arguably the single most striking result linking cosmology to everyday life.

A star spends most of its existence fusing hydrogen into helium in its core. When the hydrogen there runs out, the core contracts and heats until helium itself can fuse, which requires about 100 million kelvin and proceeds by an improbable-looking route: two helium nuclei form an unstable beryllium-8 that survives for less than a ten-thousandth of a nanosecond, just long enough for a third helium to strike it and make carbon-12. Hoyle predicted in 1953 that carbon must have an energy level at a very specific value to make this work, purely on the grounds that carbon exists; the level was found experimentally soon after, one of the few genuinely successful predictions ever made from the fact of our own existence.

In stars above roughly eight solar masses the process continues through successive shells, carbon to neon, neon to oxygen, oxygen to silicon, silicon to iron, each stage hotter, faster and shorter than the last. Silicon burning may last only a day. There the sequence stops absolutely, because iron-56 has the highest binding energy per nucleon of any nucleus: fusing iron consumes energy rather than releasing it. With no outward pressure the core collapses in under a second, rebounds, and blows the star apart as a core-collapse supernova, briefly outshining an entire galaxy.

Elements heavier than iron are made by neutron capture rather than fusion. The slow process, or s-process, operates over thousands of years in the interiors of ageing low-mass stars and builds elements up to about bismuth. The rapid process, or r-process, requires an intense neutron flux over seconds and produces gold, platinum, uranium and thorium. For decades supernovae were assumed responsible, but in August 2017 the merger of two neutron stars, detected simultaneously as gravitational waves by LIGO and as light across the spectrum, was seen to manufacture roughly the mass of several Earths in heavy elements. Neutron star mergers are now thought to be a major, perhaps dominant, source of the gold in any wedding ring.

Enrichment is cumulative, and astronomers track it as metallicity, meaning the proportion of everything heavier than helium. The Sun is about 1.5 per cent metals by mass; the oldest surviving stars have less than a ten-thousandth of that. Rocky planets could not form at all until enough generations of stars had lived and died to supply the raw material, which is one reason the Earth appears comparatively late in cosmic history.

sections.heading: The Solar System, the Earth and the Moon
sections.body:
About 4.568 billion years ago, a fragment of a molecular cloud in the outer Milky Way began to collapse, possibly nudged by the shock wave from a nearby supernova, whose short-lived radioactive debris is still detectable in the oldest meteorites. This date is known with remarkable precision because calcium-aluminium-rich inclusions, the first solids to condense in the cooling disc, can be dated by uranium-lead methods to within a few hundred thousand years. They are the oldest objects anyone has ever held.

Conservation of angular momentum flattened the collapsing cloud into a rotating disc. Roughly 99.8 per cent of the mass fell to the centre and ignited as the Sun; the remainder formed a protoplanetary disc in which temperature fell steeply with distance. Inside the frost line, at roughly three to four times the Earth-Sun distance, only metals and silicates could condense, which is why the inner planets are small, dense and rocky. Beyond it water, ammonia and methane froze, giving planetary cores far more material to work with and allowing Jupiter and Saturn to grow massive enough to capture hydrogen and helium directly. Dust grains stuck together electrostatically, centimetre lumps grew to kilometre planetesimals, and gravity then took over in runaway accretion, building planets in perhaps 10 to 100 million years.

The Earth formed at a distance where liquid water can exist at the surface, one of the clearest Goldilocks conditions in the whole story. Its mass is large enough to retain an atmosphere but not so large as to hold onto hydrogen. Radioactive decay of uranium, thorium and potassium-40 in the interior, together with heat left from accretion, keeps the planet geologically active after 4.5 billion years, driving plate tectonics, which recycles crust, regulates carbon dioxide over geological time through the weathering of silicate rock, and thereby stabilises climate over hundreds of millions of years. A convecting iron core generates a magnetic field that deflects the solar wind and helps prevent the atmosphere from being stripped away, as Mars's largely was.

The Moon is almost certainly the result of a catastrophe. About 4.5 billion years ago a body roughly the size of Mars, conventionally named Theia, struck the proto-Earth obliquely. The impact melted much of the planet and threw a disc of vaporised rock into orbit, which coalesced within perhaps a century into the Moon. The evidence is circumstantial but strong: the Moon has a very small iron core, is depleted in volatile elements, and has oxygen isotope ratios nearly identical to Earth's, implying the two are made of the same material thoroughly mixed. The Moon stabilises Earth's axial tilt at about 23.4 degrees, preventing the chaotic wobbles that would otherwise produce wild swings of climate.

sections.heading: The Origin of Life
sections.body:
Life appeared on Earth remarkably early. The oldest widely accepted fossils are stromatolites, layered mounds built by microbial mats, from the Pilbara region of Western Australia at about 3.5 billion years, and there are contested chemical traces suggesting life at 3.7 or even 4.1 billion years. Since the Earth was probably not habitable much before 4.3 billion years ago, life either arose quickly or arose repeatedly. How it arose is the largest unsolved problem in this account, and intellectual honesty requires saying that no one knows.

What is understood is the chemistry that makes the question tractable. In 1953 Stanley Miller, working with Harold Urey at Chicago, sealed water, methane, ammonia and hydrogen in glassware and passed electrical sparks through it for a week, producing several amino acids. The specific atmosphere he assumed is now thought wrong, since the early atmosphere was probably dominated by carbon dioxide and nitrogen, but the general lesson survived: the building blocks of life form readily under plausible geochemical conditions. They also arrive from space. The Murchison meteorite, which fell in Australia in 1969, contains more than seventy amino acids, and comets carry organic molecules in quantity.

The hard step is not making building blocks but getting a system that copies itself with occasional errors, since that is the minimum requirement for natural selection to begin. Modern cells face a chicken-and-egg problem: DNA stores information but needs proteins to be copied, while proteins are built from DNA instructions. The favoured escape is the RNA world hypothesis, proposed in the 1960s and strengthened by the discovery in the early 1980s that some RNA molecules, called ribozymes, can act as catalysts. RNA can therefore carry information and do chemistry, so a self-copying RNA could precede both DNA and protein. Supporting this, the ribosome, the machine that builds every protein in every living thing, turns out to have RNA rather than protein at its catalytic core, which looks like a fossil of an earlier arrangement.

Where it happened is disputed. Alkaline hydrothermal vents on the sea floor, such as the Lost City field discovered in 2000, offer natural mineral compartments, steady chemical energy and proton gradients across thin walls that resemble how all cells still make energy. Darwin's own guess of a warm little pond has been revived because wet-dry cycles concentrate molecules and drive the linking reactions that water otherwise reverses. Both remain hypotheses.

What is not in doubt is common ancestry. Every organism examined uses the same genetic code, the same twenty amino acids and the same handedness of sugars, which points to a single last universal common ancestor, LUCA, probably a population rather than an individual, living perhaps 3.8 billion years ago and already possessing genes, membranes and a metabolism.

sections.heading: Photosynthesis, Oxygen and the Transformation of a Planet
sections.body:
For its first two billion years life was microbial, invisible and chemically modest, but it was already altering the planet. The decisive innovation was oxygenic photosynthesis, evolved by the cyanobacteria at some point before 2.7 billion years ago and arguably the most consequential single invention in the history of the Earth. Earlier photosynthesisers had used hydrogen sulphide or dissolved iron as a source of electrons, both in limited supply. The cyanobacteria learned to split water instead, using the energy of sunlight to prise hydrogen from oxygen in a molecule that covers most of the planet. The supply problem vanished, and the biosphere's energy budget expanded enormously.

The waste product was oxygen, which to the anaerobic life of the time was a corrosive poison. At first it was mopped up by dissolved iron in the oceans, precipitating out as the banded iron formations that today supply most of the world's iron ore, their alternating red and grey layers laid down over hundreds of millions of years. Once that sink was saturated, oxygen began accumulating in the atmosphere in what is called the Great Oxidation Event, starting about 2.4 billion years ago. The consequences were drastic. Vast numbers of anaerobic organisms were killed or driven into the muds and deep sediments where their descendants still live, in what may have been the largest extinction the Earth has known. Oxygen also destroyed atmospheric methane, a potent greenhouse gas, and the resulting cooling is the likely trigger for the Huronian glaciation, a period of extreme ice cover lasting perhaps 300 million years.

The compensations were profound. Oxygen permits aerobic respiration, which extracts roughly fifteen to eighteen times as much usable energy from a molecule of glucose as fermentation does. That energy dividend is the precondition for everything large and active that came later; no animal could run, hunt or think on fermentation alone. High in the atmosphere, oxygen also formed ozone, which absorbs ultraviolet radiation and eventually made dry land survivable.

Oxygen levels did not rise smoothly. After the initial jump they appear to have hovered at perhaps one to a few per cent of present levels through a long, chemically sluggish interval sometimes nicknamed the boring billion, before a second major rise between roughly 800 and 540 million years ago associated with the Neoproterozoic oxygenation event. Whether that second rise caused the appearance of large animals or merely accompanied it is actively debated. This period also saw the most severe glaciations in Earth's history, the Snowball Earth episodes around 717 to 635 million years ago, when ice may have reached the tropics and possibly the equator, with life surviving in refuges beneath the ice and around volcanic vents.

sections.heading: Complex Cells, Multicellularity and the Cambrian Explosion
sections.body:
Between the microbial world and the world of visible organisms lies a threshold as sharp as any in the story: the eukaryotic cell. Bacteria and archaea, the prokaryotes, are small, simple and lack internal compartments. Eukaryotic cells, from which all plants, animals and fungi are built, are typically a thousand to ten thousand times larger by volume, contain a nucleus enclosing the chromosomes, and are filled with specialised organelles. This transition, dated somewhere between about 2.1 and 1.6 billion years ago, appears to have happened only once.

Its mechanism is one of the more surprising results in biology. Lynn Margulis argued forcefully in a 1967 paper, rejected by fifteen journals before publication, that mitochondria and chloroplasts are descended from free-living bacteria engulfed by a host cell and retained rather than digested. The evidence is now overwhelming: both organelles have their own circular DNA resembling bacterial genomes, both have double membranes as expected of an engulfed cell, both reproduce by dividing independently, and their ribosomes are bacterial in type, which is why some antibiotics have mitochondrial side effects. Mitochondria descend from an aerobic bacterium, chloroplasts from a cyanobacterium captured later. The energy that mitochondria supply, distributed across many internal membranes rather than one outer surface, is probably what allowed eukaryotic genomes to grow orders of magnitude larger than bacterial ones.

Multicellularity followed, and unlike the eukaryotic cell it evolved independently many times, at least twenty-five by most counts, including separately in animals, plants, fungi and several algal lineages. It requires cells to cooperate, to specialise, and to accept that most of them will not reproduce, which is a genuine evolutionary puzzle solved largely by close genetic relatedness among the cells of one body.

The Ediacaran biota, soft-bodied organisms up to a metre across first recognised in Australia's Ediacara Hills and dating from about 575 million years ago, are the earliest large complex organisms known, though how they relate to later animals is unresolved.

Then, beginning about 538.8 million years ago, came the Cambrian explosion. Over perhaps 20 to 25 million years, a geological eye-blink, almost all the major animal body plans alive today appear in the fossil record, along with several that did not survive. Deposits such as the Burgess Shale in British Columbia, found by Charles Walcott in 1909, and Chengjiang in China preserve the detail exquisitely. Proposed causes include the oxygen rise, the invention of predation and the resulting arms race in shells, eyes and skeletons, and the accumulation of genetic toolkits. Part of the apparent suddenness is also preservation bias: hard parts fossilise and soft bodies do not, and molecular clock estimates suggest the lineages diverged well before they became visible in the rocks. Even allowing for that, the Cambrian marks the point at which the biosphere acquired ecosystems recognisably like modern ones, with predators, prey, burrowers and swimmers arranged in food chains several levels deep.

sections.heading: Life on Land, Mass Extinction and the Rise of Mammals
sections.body:
Land was uninhabitable until the ozone layer thickened enough to block ultraviolet radiation, and even then colonising it meant solving desiccation, gravity and reproduction without water. Plants managed it first, arriving from freshwater algae around 470 million years ago and evolving in sequence a waxy cuticle to retain water, stomata to admit carbon dioxide, vascular tissue to move fluid upward, and lignin, which is stiff enough to support a trunk. By the Carboniferous, roughly 359 to 299 million years ago, forests of tree-sized club mosses and horsetails covered swampy continents, and because lignin-digesting fungi had not yet become efficient, much of that timber was buried rather than rotted. It became the coal that would, three hundred million years later, power industrial civilisation.

Arthropods followed the plants ashore, and vertebrates followed the arthropods, with lobe-finned fish evolving weight-bearing limbs by about 375 million years ago in animals such as Tiktaalik, discovered in the Canadian Arctic in 2004. Amphibians remained tethered to water for reproduction until the amniotic egg, with its own private pond sealed inside a shell, freed reptiles to colonise dry interiors.

The history of life on land is punctuated by catastrophe. Five mass extinctions are conventionally recognised. The end-Permian event 251.9 million years ago is the worst, eliminating an estimated 81 to 96 per cent of marine species, with the Siberian Traps eruptions, which flooded some seven million cubic kilometres of lava and released colossal quantities of carbon dioxide and sulphur, the leading suspect. Recovery took perhaps ten million years. The end-Cretaceous event 66 million years ago is the best understood: a bolide about ten kilometres across struck the Yucatán, excavating the 180 kilometre Chicxulub crater, and the iridium-rich clay layer it left behind was identified worldwide by Luis and Walter Alvarez in 1980. Global fires, a plunge into cold and darkness lasting years, and acidified oceans killed roughly three quarters of species, including all non-avian dinosaurs.

Mass extinctions are usually described as tragedies, and they are, but they are also the mechanism by which the biosphere is repeatedly reshuffled. Mammals had existed alongside dinosaurs for well over 150 million years, mostly small, nocturnal and insectivorous, occupying the niches large reptiles left over. Within about ten million years of Chicxulub they had radiated into large herbivores, carnivores, whales and primates. The primates, arboreal and grasping, developed forward-facing eyes for judging distance among branches, hands capable of precise manipulation, and comparatively large brains. Roughly seven million years ago, in an Africa that was drying and giving way from forest to mosaic woodland and savannah, one primate lineage began habitually walking upright.

It is worth noticing how contingent this is. Had the Chicxulub impactor arrived a few minutes earlier or later, it would have struck deep ocean rather than the sulphur-rich shallow carbonates of the Yucatán, and the climatic aftermath might have been far milder. Nothing in the physics of the preceding thirteen billion years made mammals, primates or people inevitable.

sections.heading: Human Origins: Upright Walking, Big Brains and Fire
sections.body:
The hominin lineage separated from that of chimpanzees between roughly 7 and 6 million years ago, a date estimated from genetic differences and consistent with fossils such as Sahelanthropus tchadensis from Chad, dated to about 7 million years. Contrary to intuition, the large brain came late. Bipedalism came first, and it came first by a wide margin.

Australopithecus afarensis, represented by the celebrated partial skeleton nicknamed Lucy found at Hadar in Ethiopia by Donald Johanson in 1974 and dated to 3.2 million years, walked fully upright on a human-like pelvis and arched foot while carrying a brain of about 400 to 500 cubic centimetres, barely larger than a chimpanzee's. The Laetoli footprints in Tanzania, discovered by Mary Leakey's team in 1976 and preserved in volcanic ash 3.6 million years old, show the striding gait unambiguously. Upright walking is energetically cheaper over long distances, raises the head above tall grass, and above all frees the hands, but the fossil record shows it was not immediately accompanied by cleverness.

Brains enlarged later and rapidly. Homo habilis, from about 2.4 million years ago, reached some 600 cubic centimetres and is associated with the Oldowan stone tools that give the period its name, simple sharp-edged flakes struck from cobbles. Homo erectus, appearing about 1.9 million years ago, reached 900 cubic centimetres or more, had modern body proportions, made the more demanding teardrop-shaped Acheulean handaxe, and was the first hominin to leave Africa, reaching Georgia by 1.8 million years and Java and China soon after. Homo sapiens arrived with roughly 1,350 cubic centimetres, more than triple the australopithecine figure.

Brains are metabolically ruinous. The human brain is about 2 per cent of body weight but consumes around 20 per cent of resting energy. Paying for it required a better diet, and fire is the leading explanation. Richard Wrangham's cooking hypothesis argues that controlled fire, for which there is reasonable evidence at Wonderwerk Cave in South Africa a million years ago and unambiguous evidence by 400,000 years ago, externalised part of digestion. Cooking gelatinises starch, denatures protein and softens fibre, raising the energy extracted from food and cutting chewing time from the six hours a chimpanzee spends to under an hour. Human guts shrank while brains grew, a trade sometimes called the expensive tissue hypothesis.

Africa remained the centre. Fossils from Jebel Irhoud in Morocco, redated in 2017 to about 315,000 years, are the earliest widely accepted Homo sapiens. Modern humans then expanded out of Africa, with the major dispersal around 60,000 to 70,000 years ago, interbreeding with Neanderthals and Denisovans as they went; most people outside Africa carry roughly 1 to 2 per cent Neanderthal DNA, and some populations in Oceania carry several per cent Denisovan ancestry, including a variant that assists high-altitude living in Tibet.

sections.heading: Collective Learning and the Palaeolithic World
sections.body:
Big History gives humans their own threshold, and the justification is a single capacity: collective learning. Many animals learn, and several, including chimpanzees, crows and whales, transmit local traditions. What humans do differently is accumulate. Because human language can encode an unlimited number of precise, novel propositions, including statements about things absent, hypothetical or abstract, information can pass between individuals and across generations faster than it is lost. Each generation therefore starts from a larger inherited stock than the last, and the store of shared knowledge ratchets upward. No other species has a comparable ratchet, which is why chimpanzee toolkits look much the same today as a century ago while human toolkits do not.

The consequence is that human history is driven by cultural rather than genetic change, and cultural change is orders of magnitude faster. A genetic adaptation to cold requires many generations; a coat requires an afternoon. This is why one anatomically unchanged species came to occupy tundra, desert, rainforest and mountain within a few tens of thousands of years, without evolving specialised bodies for any of them.

The evidence of accumulating culture becomes conspicuous in the Upper Palaeolithic after about 50,000 years ago, though the pattern in Africa reaches back much further and the notion of a sudden revolution is now widely doubted. Stone tools become specialised and regionally distinctive; bone, antler and ivory are worked; the spearthrower, the bow, the eyed needle, the oil lamp and the fish hook appear. So does art of extraordinary sophistication, including the painted caves of Chauvet in France at about 36,000 years and Lascaux at about 17,000 years, ivory figurines from Hohle Fels in Germany at 40,000 years, and the ochre hand stencils of Sulawesi in Indonesia dated to at least 39,000 years. Burial with grave goods implies belief; ornaments made of shells carried hundreds of kilometres inland imply exchange networks.

Palaeolithic people lived in small mobile bands, typically of perhaps 25 to 50 individuals, foraging over large territories and aggregating seasonally. Ethnographic and archaeological evidence suggests they were healthier and less overworked than the farmers who followed, with a varied diet and, in favourable regions, working days measured in a handful of hours. They were not, however, gentle on other species. Human arrival correlates closely with the extinction of large animals: most of Australia's giant marsupials disappeared within a few thousand years of settlement around 50,000 years ago, and the Americas lost mammoths, mastodons, giant sloths and sabre-toothed cats after human arrival roughly 15,000 years ago, with climate change at the end of the last glacial period a contributing and much-debated factor. Africa, where large animals had co-evolved with hominins over millions of years and had time to learn wariness, kept most of its megafauna, which is itself an argument that human hunting mattered.

sections.heading: Agriculture and the Holocene Bargain
sections.body:
For 200,000 years humans foraged. Then, within a few thousand years, farming appeared independently in at least seven and probably eleven separate regions: the Fertile Crescent from about 11,000 years ago with wheat, barley, sheep and goats; China with rice and millet by 9,000 years ago; Mesoamerica with maize, beans and squash; the Andes with potatoes and llamas; New Guinea with taro and banana; West Africa with sorghum and yams; and eastern North America with local seed crops. Independent invention on separate continents within a narrow window demands a common cause.

The cause was almost certainly climate. The Pleistocene ice ages were not merely cold but violently unstable, with temperature swings of several degrees within decades and atmospheric carbon dioxide low enough, around 180 to 200 parts per million, to limit plant growth. Around 11,700 years ago the Holocene began, and the climate became unusually warm, wet and, above all, stable, staying within roughly one degree for ten millennia. Farming requires betting a year of labour on a predictable harvest, and only the Holocene made that bet reasonable.

Domestication was a slow mutual process rather than an invention. Humans selected, mostly unconsciously, for traits convenient to them: cereals whose seed heads did not shatter and scatter, seeds that germinated together, larger fruit, animals that tolerated crowding and bred in captivity. Those traits were disastrous for the plants and animals in the wild but spectacularly successful in partnership, and the species involved now number in the billions.

The bargain was harsh for most individuals. Skeletal evidence across many regions shows early farmers were shorter than the foragers who preceded them, by perhaps 10 to 15 centimetres in some sequences, with worse teeth, more anaemia, more spinal damage from grinding grain, and more infectious disease. Diets narrowed to a few starchy staples. Living beside animals in dense settlements created the conditions for zoonotic disease to jump species and become endemic, giving humanity measles, smallpox, influenza and tuberculosis. Farming also demanded more hours of harder labour.

What farming did deliver was calories per hectare, perhaps ten to a hundred times what foraging could extract from the same land, and therefore population. World population rose from perhaps 5 to 10 million at the end of the last ice age to around 250 million by the year one of the common era. Denser populations meant more minds in contact, so collective learning accelerated. Storable surplus meant that some people could stop producing food, which made possible priests, soldiers, artisans, scribes and rulers, and also made possible the systematic inequality that follows from someone controlling the store. Almost everything conventionally called civilisation follows from a grain silo. Grain in particular suits a ruler's purposes, since it ripens predictably, can be measured, stored and taxed, and cannot be hidden underground as tubers can, which may be part of why cereal societies produced states and root-crop societies often did not.

sections.heading: Cities, States, Writing and Empires
sections.body:
Where farming produced reliable surpluses, particularly in the irrigated floodplains of large rivers, settlements grew into cities and cities into states. Uruk in southern Mesopotamia may have held 40,000 to 80,000 people by 3000 BCE. Comparable developments followed along the Nile, the Indus, the Yellow River, and independently in Mesoamerica and the Andes, which is important evidence that states are a repeatable response to certain conditions rather than a single cultural accident.

Writing emerged from accounting rather than literature. The earliest Mesopotamian tablets, from Uruk around 3200 BCE, are administrative records of grain, sheep and beer, descended from a much older system of clay tokens used to track goods. Only later was the script bent to law, myth and poetry. Writing is a threshold in its own right for collective learning: speech is limited by memory and by the number of people within earshot, while a written record transmits precisely across centuries and continents. Independent invention occurred in Egypt around 3200 BCE, in China by about 1200 BCE, and among the Maya by around 300 BCE.
