guides.summary: An introduction to environmental history, the study of how human societies and the natural world have shaped each other over time, covering the field's methods and archives, the major transformations from the Pleistocene extinctions to the Great Acceleration, and the debates that define the discipline today.

sections.heading: What Environmental History Is and Why It Exists
sections.body:
Environmental history is the study of how human societies and the rest of the natural world have shaped each other across time. It differs from conventional history in one decisive move: it treats soil, climate, disease organisms, rivers, animals and energy flows not as scenery behind the human drama but as active participants with histories of their own. A conventional account of the fall of a dynasty examines succession disputes, taxation and armies. An environmental historian asks in addition what the harvests were doing, whether the summers had turned cold, what a new pathogen was doing to the population, and where the fuel and the fertility to sustain a capital city were coming from. Neither account is complete on its own; the argument of the field is that the second set of questions has been systematically neglected and that answering them changes the story.

The field is usually described as having three interlocking levels of enquiry. The first is the material level: reconstructing what the environment actually was and how it changed, which requires evidence from the natural sciences. The second is the political-economic level: how societies organised production, property, labour and technology to extract from that environment, and how power was distributed in the process. The third is the intellectual and cultural level: what people believed nature was, what they thought it was for, and how those beliefs licensed or restrained what they did to it. The historian Donald Worster proposed this triad in the 1980s and it remains a serviceable map of the discipline.

The field emerged as a self-conscious enterprise in the early 1970s, and it is not a coincidence that this was the moment of the first Earth Day, the founding of national environmental agencies, and the publication of the Club of Rome's report The Limits to Growth in 1972. Roderick Nash used the phrase environmental history in a 1972 essay describing it as a new teaching frontier, and the American Society for Environmental History was founded in 1977. A European counterpart followed in 1999, and today national and regional associations exist across Asia, Africa and Latin America. The field grew out of a present-day anxiety, which is both its origin and one of its persistent methodological hazards.

The practical claim of the discipline is that many questions people care about now are historical questions in disguise. Whether a fishery can recover depends on what its baseline abundance actually was, which is a documentary and archaeological problem before it is a biological one. Whether a drought produces famine depends on entitlements, storage and trade, which are historical arrangements. Whether a landscape is natural or the product of millennia of human burning and cultivation is a question that determines what restoring it would even mean. Environmental history supplies the long time series against which present conditions can be judged, and it repeatedly demonstrates that intuitions about what is normal are calibrated to a very short and often unrepresentative slice of the past.

sections.heading: Intellectual Foundations and the Field's Formative Texts
sections.body:
The intellectual ancestry of environmental history runs back well before the 1970s. George Perkins Marsh, an American diplomat and philologist who had watched Vermont hillsides erode after clearance and then toured the deforested Mediterranean, published Man and Nature in 1864. Its central argument, that human action had already transformed the earth on a scale and with a permanence that people refused to acknowledge, and that deforestation in particular set off cascading damage to soils, streams and climate, reads as strikingly modern. Lewis Mumford later called it the fountainhead of the conservation movement.

A second lineage runs through the French Annales school. Fernand Braudel's The Mediterranean and the Mediterranean World in the Age of Philip II, published in 1949, divided history into three tempos: the almost motionless time of geography and climate, the slower rhythms of economies and social structures, and the rapid froth of political events. Braudel's insistence that mountains, sea currents and olive cultivation were causally prior to kings gave later environmental historians both a model and a warning about how far to push structural explanation. Emmanuel Le Roy Ladurie extended the approach directly into climate with Times of Feast, Times of Famine in 1967, mining wine-harvest dates and glacier records to reconstruct European temperatures.

The founding texts of the field proper appeared in a remarkable fifteen-year burst. Alfred Crosby's The Columbian Exchange in 1972 recast 1492 as a biological event. Donald Worster's Dust Bowl in 1979 read the 1930s southern plains catastrophe as the predictable outcome of a capitalist agricultural culture applied to a semi-arid grassland, and his Rivers of Empire in 1985 analysed the American West as a hydraulic society organised around the control of water. Carolyn Merchant's The Death of Nature in 1980 traced how the Scientific Revolution replaced an organic, feminised image of nature with a mechanical one available for domination. William Cronon's Changes in the Land in 1983 showed how the imposition of English property regimes on New England ecosystems transformed both, and remains the most widely assigned book in the field.

From the late 1980s the field decisively globalised. Ramachandra Guha's The Unquiet Woods in 1989 examined peasant resistance to colonial forestry in the Indian Himalaya and, with Madhav Gadgil, insisted that environmentalism in the global South was primarily a livelihood struggle rather than an aesthetic one. Joan Martínez-Alier later named this the environmentalism of the poor. J. R. McNeill's Something New Under the Sun, published in 2000, offered the first synthetic environmental history of the twentieth century and argued that the scale and speed of change after 1945 constituted a genuine break rather than an intensification. Together these works established that environmental history could be written as political history, as economic history, as intellectual history, and at any scale from a single watershed to the planet.

sections.heading: Reading Nature's Archive: Sources, Proxies and Dating
sections.body:
The distinctive methodological problem of environmental history is that its subject leaves records in two incompatible languages. One is the written archive: estate accounts, tithe records, ship logs, administrative surveys, travellers' descriptions, court cases over water rights, newspaper reports of floods. The other is the physical archive, which must be read through proxies, measurable quantities that vary with a past condition of interest. Competence in the field means being able to work with both and, crucially, knowing the error structure of each.

Dendrochronology, the study of tree rings, was placed on a rigorous footing by the astronomer A. E. Douglass in the first decades of the twentieth century. In climates where a single factor limits growth, ring width varies with that factor, so a sequence of wide and narrow rings forms a pattern that can be matched, or crossdated, between living trees, dead timber and archaeological beams, extending year-by-year chronologies back thousands of years. Some bristlecone pine and oak chronologies now run beyond ten thousand years. Because rings are annual and absolutely dated, they are the gold standard against which other proxies are calibrated.

Palynology, pioneered by the Swedish geologist Lennart von Post in 1916, extracts pollen grains from waterlogged sediments in lakes and peat bogs. Pollen walls are made of sporopollenin and survive for millennia, and each plant family produces a recognisable grain, so a core provides a stratified record of the surrounding vegetation. A sudden fall in tree pollen accompanied by a rise in cereal and weed pollen and a spike in microscopic charcoal is the classic signature of forest clearance for agriculture. Ice cores from Greenland and Antarctica trap actual samples of ancient atmosphere in bubbles: the EPICA core from Dome C reaches back about 800,000 years and gives direct measurements of past carbon dioxide and methane, alongside oxygen isotope ratios that indicate temperature, and layers of volcanic sulphate and industrial lead that date eruptions and pollution.

Absolute dating rests substantially on radiocarbon, developed by Willard Libby in 1949 and recognised with a Nobel Prize in 1960. Living things maintain the atmospheric ratio of radioactive carbon-14 to stable carbon; at death intake stops and carbon-14 decays with a half-life of 5,730 years, giving usable dates to roughly 50,000 years. Raw radiocarbon years must be calibrated against tree-ring records because atmospheric carbon-14 production has varied, and marine samples require a reservoir correction. Other tools include stable isotope ratios in bone and shell for diet and temperature, varve counting in annually layered lake sediments, luminescence dating of buried sediment grains, and increasingly ancient DNA recovered from bones and even from sediment itself. Each proxy answers a narrow question with a specific uncertainty, and the discipline's characteristic error is to press a proxy to say more than its resolution permits.

sections.heading: Deep Time: Human Arrival and the Pleistocene Extinctions
sections.body:
The first chapter of environmental history predates agriculture, writing and cities. Over the last fifty thousand years the world lost most of its very large land animals in a pattern that is difficult to explain without reference to humans. Australia lost some ninety percent of its megafaunal genera, including the two-tonne wombat relative Diprotodon and the giant flightless bird Genyornis, in a window centred around 46,000 to 40,000 years ago that closely follows human arrival. The Americas lost roughly seventy percent of large mammal genera between about 14,000 and 10,000 years ago, among them mammoths, mastodons, giant ground sloths, glyptodonts, native horses, camels, and the predators that depended on them. Madagascar and New Zealand, colonised only in the last two millennia, lost elephant birds and moa within a few centuries of human landfall.

The overkill hypothesis, argued most forcefully by Paul Martin from 1967, holds that these animals had never encountered a cooperative, projectile-armed hunter and had no behavioural defences, and that even modest sustained hunting pressure on slow-reproducing species drives extinction. The suspicious correlation with human arrival dates, rather than with any single climatic event, is its strongest evidence, as is the survival of African megafauna where large mammals co-evolved with hominins over millions of years and had time to acquire wariness. The competing climate hypothesis points to the abrupt warming and vegetation reorganisation at the end of the last glacial period, particularly the Bølling-Allerød warming and the Younger Dryas cold snap between roughly 12,900 and 11,700 years ago.

The current state of the debate is genuinely unresolved and probably favours a combination. Radiocarbon dating has been refined enough to show that the timing varies by continent, that some extinctions are poorly synchronised with human arrival, and that many species had already been reduced by climate-driven range contraction before people appeared. The most defensible summary is that climatic stress and human predation acted together, with the relative weight differing by place and species, and that megafauna which had survived many previous glacial cycles unharmed failed to survive the one that included humans.

The consequences reached beyond the lost animals. Large herbivores are ecosystem engineers: they trample and browse woody growth, disperse seeds, and cycle nutrients across landscapes in their dung and carcasses. Their removal is thought to have shifted vegetation toward denser woodland in some regions and reduced long-distance nutrient transport substantially. In Australia the loss of large browsers may have increased fuel loads and helped establish the fire-dominated regime that Aboriginal societies then managed deliberately for tens of thousands of years. The deeper lesson for the discipline is that there is no pre-human baseline available for most of the inhabited world. By the time agriculture began, humans had already restructured the terrestrial fauna of every continent except Africa, and the ecosystems that later observers would call pristine were already post-human artefacts.

sections.heading: The Agricultural Transition and Its Ecological Consequences
sections.body:
The shift from foraging to farming is the largest single change in the human relationship with the rest of nature, and it happened independently in at least eleven regions over several thousand years. The oldest well-documented centre is the Fertile Crescent, where einkorn and emmer wheat, barley, lentils, peas and flax were domesticated from about 11,500 years ago, followed by goats, sheep, pigs and cattle. Rice and millet were domesticated in China from around 9,000 years ago, maize in southern Mexico from teosinte over a long process beginning around 9,000 years ago, potatoes and quinoa in the Andes, sorghum and pearl millet in the African Sahel, taro and banana in New Guinea, and squash and goosefoot in eastern North America. That agriculture arose repeatedly and independently within a few thousand years of the end of the Pleistocene is strong evidence that the stable, warm, wetter and unusually predictable climate of the early Holocene was a necessary precondition.

Domestication is a biological process with recognisable signatures. Under human selection, cereals lose the brittle rachis that shatters seed heads for natural dispersal, because only plants whose seed stays attached get harvested and resown; seeds enlarge and dormancy weakens. Animals under domestication show a consistent syndrome of reduced body and brain size, shortened faces, floppy ears, patchy coats and delayed development, plausibly linked to selection for tameness acting on neural crest cells. These changes are visible in the archaeological record and allow domestication to be dated.

The environmental consequences were profound and largely negative for the individuals involved. Skeletal evidence from many early farming populations shows shorter stature, more dental caries from starchy diets, more anaemia and more infectious disease than in neighbouring foragers, since farming concentrates people in permanent settlements alongside domestic animals and their parasites. Measles, smallpox, influenza and tuberculosis all have origins in or close relationships with herd animal diseases, and required populations dense enough to sustain them. What agriculture provided was not health but calories per hectare, and therefore numbers.

Cleared, tilled land also behaves differently from forest and grassland. Bare soil between crops erodes at rates commonly one to two orders of magnitude above natural background. Irrigation in arid regions raises water tables and evaporation leaves dissolved salts behind. The best-documented case comes from southern Mesopotamia, where cuneiform records analysed by Thorkild Jacobsen and Robert Adams in 1958 show wheat falling from about half the crop around 3500 BCE to under two percent by 2100 BCE as farmers switched to salt-tolerant barley, alongside reported yield declines of roughly two-thirds over the same span. Whether salinisation caused political collapse or merely accompanied it remains argued, but the record is a clear early demonstration that intensive agriculture can degrade the resource it depends on within a few centuries.

sections.heading: Forests, Water and Soil in the Ancient and Medieval World
sections.body:
Pre-industrial societies ran on what the economic historian E. A. Wrigley called an organic economy: essentially all energy and materials derived from recent photosynthesis, whether as food, fodder for draught animals, firewood, charcoal, or timber. Since photosynthesis is limited by land area, the ceiling on such an economy is a land ceiling, and its characteristic environmental crisis is a shortage of wood. Mediterranean antiquity provides the earliest sustained record. Plato, in the Critias, described the hills of Attica as the bones of a wasted body, stripped of soil that had once supported great trees, and while the passage is a moral argument rather than a survey, pollen and sediment evidence broadly supports extensive Classical-era clearance for cropland, shipbuilding, and the enormous fuel demands of metallurgy, ceramics and public baths.

Roman silver and lead smelting at Rio Tinto in Iberia and elsewhere left a measurable signature: lead concentrations in Greenland ice cores rise sharply from about 600 BCE, peak in the first and second centuries CE at several times natural background, and collapse after the third century, tracking imperial mining output. This is one of the cleanest demonstrations that ancient industry operated at a hemispheric scale, and it also shows how a physical archive can be used to date an economic downturn independent of texts.

Medieval Europe experienced a long agricultural expansion between roughly 1000 and 1300, driven by the heavy mouldboard plough, the horse collar, three-field rotation and watermills, and enabled by the relatively mild Medieval Climate Anomaly. Forest cover in France and Germany fell substantially as assarting pushed cultivation onto marginal land. England's Domesday Book of 1086 already records a landscape only about fifteen percent wooded, with some 6,000 watermills. Expansion onto poor soils left the system with no reserve, and when a run of catastrophically wet years arrived, the Great Famine of 1315 to 1322 killed perhaps ten to fifteen percent of northern Europe's population before the Black Death arrived in 1347.

Water management produced the era's most impressive engineering and its most durable political structures. Terraced rice landscapes in China and Southeast Asia, the qanat underground channels of Iran, the falaj of Oman, and the tank irrigation systems of southern India and Sri Lanka each represent centuries of accumulated design under specific hydrological constraints. Karl Wittfogel's 1957 hydraulic hypothesis, which argued that large-scale irrigation required and produced despotic bureaucratic states, has been largely rejected in that strong form, since many productive systems were built and maintained by local cooperative institutions with no central authority. The revised understanding, developed by scholars including Elinor Ostrom, is that durable commons management depends on clear boundaries, locally made rules, graduated sanctions and cheap conflict resolution, not on coercion from above.

sections.heading: The Columbian Exchange and Ecological Imperialism
sections.body:
For roughly a hundred million years the biota of the Americas had evolved in isolation from those of Afro-Eurasia. Alfred Crosby's argument, set out in The Columbian Exchange in 1972 and extended in Ecological Imperialism in 1986, is that the voyages beginning in 1492 reconnected these separated evolutionary experiments and that the resulting biological traffic reshaped the world more thoroughly than any political event of the period. The exchange moved in both directions and its effects were profoundly asymmetric.

Travelling east from the Americas were maize, potatoes, sweet potatoes, cassava, tomatoes, chilli peppers, beans, squash, peanuts, cacao, tobacco, rubber and quinine. Several of these are calorically superior to what they replaced on marginal land: potatoes yield more energy per hectare than grain on cool wet soils, and maize and cassava tolerate conditions that defeat wheat and rice. Historians have credited these crops with a substantial share of the population growth of eighteenth and nineteenth century Europe, China and Africa, though the causal weight is debated and monoculture dependence carried its own risk, as the Irish famine of 1845 to 1852 demonstrated when Phytophthora infestans arrived and roughly a million people died.

Travelling west were wheat, barley, rice, sugar cane, coffee, bananas and citrus, along with horses, cattle, pigs, sheep, goats and chickens. Crosby emphasised that these arrived as a package with weeds, earthworms, rats and pathogens, which he called portmanteau biota, and that the package was startlingly successful in temperate regions that resembled Europe climatically. He named these the neo-Europes, including North America, the southern cone of South America, Australia, New Zealand and parts of South Africa, and argued that European settlement succeeded there less through military superiority than through the wholesale replacement of native ecosystems by a European agricultural biota that arrived self-propelled.

Free-ranging livestock proved among the most transformative agents. Pigs released on Caribbean islands and cattle on the Mexican plateau multiplied without predators or fences, destroyed Indigenous field systems, and converted diverse vegetation into pasture within decades. Sugar plantations drove deforestation on a scale that can be dated precisely: Barbados, densely wooded when the English arrived in 1627, was effectively stripped of forest by the 1660s and thereafter imported fuel and food. The plantation complex coupled that ecological simplification to the transatlantic slave trade, which forcibly moved some twelve million people and constitutes one of the clearest cases in which environmental and human exploitation were structurally the same process. Silver mining at Potosí from 1545, using mercury from Huancavelica in the amalgamation process, poisoned watersheds and workers while injecting bullion that reorganised trade from Seville to Manila to Canton. The Columbian Exchange is thus the field's founding demonstration that globalisation was ecological before it was economic.

sections.heading: Disease, Demographic Collapse and the Landscape It Left
sections.body:
The most lethal component of the Columbian Exchange was invisible. Afro-Eurasian populations had lived for millennia in dense settlements with domestic herd animals, and had acquired both the crowd diseases that such conditions sustain and a degree of population-level immunity to them through repeated childhood exposure. The Americas had fewer domesticable herd animals, and although Indigenous societies had their own pathogens, they had no experience of smallpox, measles, influenza, typhus or, later, yellow fever and malaria. When these arrived in a population with no acquired immunity, they struck adults as severely as children, disabling the very people needed to nurse the sick, plant crops and organise defence.

The first documented smallpox epidemic reached Hispaniola in 1518 and Mexico in 1520, and successive waves of different diseases followed for more than a century, each hitting a population already reduced by the last. In the Basin of Mexico, epidemics of 1545 and 1576, known as cocoliztli and possibly caused by an indigenous haemorrhagic fever amplified by drought and by the social devastation of conquest, killed further enormous numbers. Estimates of the total decline are contested and depend on pre-contact population figures that cannot be measured directly, but a widely cited range has the hemispheric population falling from something like fifty to sixty million in 1492 to five or six million by 1600, a loss on the order of ninety percent. Lower pre-contact estimates yield smaller absolute losses but similar proportions.

This depopulation had a measurable environmental signature. Fields, orchards and managed forests across the Americas were abandoned and reverted to woody vegetation, drawing carbon out of the atmosphere. Antarctic ice cores record a distinct dip in atmospheric carbon dioxide of roughly seven to ten parts per million centred on about 1610. Simon Lewis and Mark Maslin proposed in 2015 that this Orbis spike be adopted as the formal start of the Anthropocene, precisely because it is a globally synchronous, ice-recorded marker produced by a human event. The proposal is contested, and other researchers attribute part of the dip to independent climate variability, but the underlying finding that continental-scale reforestation followed genocide and epidemic is well supported.

The consequence for how later Europeans perceived the Americas was equally significant. Settlers arriving in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries encountered forests, game-rich lands and apparently empty country, and concluded they were seeing wilderness untouched by human hands. The geographer William Denevan named this the pristine myth in a landmark 1992 essay, arguing that what Europeans saw was a landscape recovering from catastrophe, and that the Americas of 1492 had been intensively managed through burning, cultivation, earthworks and arboriculture. The myth had legal force: the doctrine that unused land was available for the taking rested on it.

sections.heading: Coal, Steam and the Break with the Organic Economy
sections.body:
Every society before roughly 1800 was constrained by the annual flow of solar energy captured by plants. Fuel, food, fodder, fibre and construction timber all competed for the same finite land, so growth in any one sector had to come at the expense of another. The decisive rupture was the substitution of fossil energy, which represents hundreds of millions of years of accumulated photosynthesis released over a few centuries. E. A. Wrigley framed this as the transition from an organic to a mineral-based economy, and it is the single most consequential development in the environmental history of the last thousand years.

Britain's transition can be traced in numbers. English coal output rose from roughly 200,000 tons a year around 1550 to about 3 million tons by 1700 and roughly 225 million tons by 1900. The proximate driver was a genuine fuel shortage: London's woodland hinterland could not supply a growing city, and coal from the Tyne, awkward and dirty though it was, became competitive. Mining below the water table then created a pumping problem, which Thomas Newcomen's atmospheric engine of 1712 solved by burning coal at the pithead to lift water out of coal mines, a self-reinforcing arrangement of remarkable elegance. James Watt's separate condenser, patented in 1769, cut fuel consumption by roughly three-quarters and made steam power economic away from coalfields; his rotative engine of 1781 extended it from pumping to driving machinery.

The environmental effects were immediate and local before they were global. Coal-burning cities produced smoke, sulphur dioxide and soot at concentrations that killed. London's air had been notorious since the seventeenth century, when John Evelyn's pamphlet Fumifugium of 1661 proposed moving industry out of the city, and the pattern culminated in the Great Smog of December 1952, when an anticyclonic inversion trapped emissions for five days and caused an estimated four to twelve thousand excess deaths, prompting the British Clean Air Act of 1956. Coal mining itself produced subsidence, acid drainage that sterilised streams, and appalling occupational disease.

The global effect was slower to appear but larger. Burning fossil carbon returns to the atmosphere carbon that had been sequestered for geological time. Svante Arrhenius calculated in 1896 that doubling atmospheric carbon dioxide would warm the earth by several degrees, arriving at figures not far from modern estimates, though he expected the process to take millennia and regarded a warmer Sweden as desirable. Carbon dioxide stood near 280 parts per million before industrialisation, was measured at 315 parts per million when Charles David Keeling began continuous observations at Mauna Loa in 1958, and has since passed 420. The Keeling Curve, with its annual sawtooth from Northern Hemisphere plant growth superimposed on a relentless rise, is arguably the single most important dataset in environmental history.

sections.heading: Commodity Frontiers, Empire and the Extraction of the Periphery
sections.body:
Industrial cores did not draw only on their own hinterlands. A recurring structure in modern environmental history is the commodity frontier: a zone where a single valuable substance is extracted rapidly and often destructively, with profits accumulating elsewhere and ecological and social costs remaining behind. Frontiers exhaust and move, leaving depleted landscapes and reorganised societies.

Peruvian guano is the clearest case. Millennia of seabird droppings had accumulated on the rainless Chincha Islands to depths of thirty metres or more, forming a fertiliser of extraordinary nitrogen and phosphorus content. Between roughly 1840 and 1880 some twelve million tons were shipped to Britain, the United States and continental Europe, restoring exhausted farmland and generating perhaps sixty percent of Peruvian state revenue at the peak. The digging was done substantially by indentured Chinese labourers under conditions widely described as lethal. The deposits were effectively exhausted within four decades, and the United States Congress passed the Guano Islands Act in 1856 authorising citizens to claim any unoccupied guano island for the nation, an early instance of resource anxiety producing territorial expansion.

Amazonian rubber followed the same arc. The vulcanisation of natural latex and the growth of bicycle and then automobile tyre demand created a boom from about 1879 to 1912 that built opera houses in Manaus and produced systematic atrocities in the Putumayo, where the Peruvian Amazon Company enslaved and killed Indigenous rubber tappers on a scale investigated by Roger Casement in 1910. The boom ended when plantations in Malaya and Ceylon, grown from seeds taken by Henry Wickham to Kew Gardens in 1876, came into production and undercut wild collection. King Leopold's Congo Free State ran a comparable rubber regime with comparable violence. Cotton, analysed by Sven Beckert as a system he calls war capitalism, linked slave-worked land in the American South, forcibly restructured cultivation in India and Egypt, and mills in Lancashire into a single ecological and economic circuit.

Marine frontiers followed the same logic with even less restraint. Nineteenth-century sperm and right whaling depleted stock after stock; twentieth-century factory ships with stern slipways and explosive harpoons then killed well over two million whales in the Southern Ocean, moving down through blue, fin, sei and finally minke whales as each was exhausted, a textbook instance of what fisheries scientists call serial depletion. On land, the North American bison fell from perhaps thirty million to a few hundred wild animals by 1889, driven by a hide market, railway access, and explicit military interest in destroying the subsistence base of Plains societies. The passenger pigeon, possibly the most numerous bird on earth at three to five billion, went from commercial harvest to extinction with the death of Martha at Cincinnati Zoo in 1914, demonstrating that abundance alone confers no protection against industrial harvest.

sections.heading: Conservation, Preservation and the Invention of Wilderness
sections.body:
Organised environmental protection emerged in the nineteenth century from several distinct and sometimes conflicting motives. Colonial administrations were among the earliest movers, for reasons more practical than sentimental. Richard Grove's work on green imperialism showed that observations on small tropical islands, where the link between deforestation and drying streams was visible within a human lifetime, produced the first state conservation measures, including forest protection on Mauritius from the 1760s. The Indian Forest Department, established in 1864 with German-trained foresters, brought a scientific sustained-yield model that also expropriated customary rights of forest-dwelling communities, generating resistance that Ramachandra Guha traced through to the twentieth-century Chipko movement.

In the United States the movement split into two wings whose disagreement still structures debate. Utilitarian conservation, embodied by Gifford Pinchot, first chief of the Forest Service from 1905, held that resources should be managed scientifically for the greatest good of the greatest number over the longest time, which meant efficient use rather than non-use. Preservationism, embodied by John Muir, founder of the Sierra Club in 1892, held that wild places had spiritual and aesthetic value that use would destroy. The two collided over the damming of Hetch Hetchy Valley inside Yosemite National Park to supply San Francisco with water, authorised in 1913 after a national controversy that Muir lost and that arguably created the American environmental movement as a political force.

The national park model, beginning with Yellowstone in 1872, was exported worldwide and carried an assumption that has since been heavily criticised: that protection requires the removal of people. Yellowstone's establishment was followed by the exclusion of Shoshone, Crow and other peoples who had hunted and burned there; Yosemite's Ahwahneechee were removed; and the same template later displaced communities across Africa and Asia, producing what critics call fortress conservation and conservation refugees. The paradox is that many of the landscapes being preserved as untouched had been produced by millennia of Indigenous management, particularly through deliberate burning, and their protection from people frequently degraded the very qualities being protected as fire-adapted systems accumulated fuel and meadows filled with brush.

William Cronon crystallised this critique in his 1995 essay The Trouble with Wilderness, arguing that wilderness is a cultural construction with a datable history, born of Romanticism and the American frontier myth, and that locating authentic nature only in places without people makes the ordinary landscapes where people actually live seem not worth defending. The essay provoked furious responses from activists who read it as undermining protection, and the exchange remains the clearest illustration of the tension between the field's analytical impulse to historicise everything and the political uses to which its conclusions are put. Cronon's own position was that recognising the idea's history should widen the circle of what deserves care rather than narrow it.

sections.heading: The Great Acceleration: Chemistry, Energy and Speed After 1945
sections.body:
J. R. McNeill's central claim about the twentieth century is that its environmental history is discontinuous with everything before it, not because the kinds of impact were new but because the rates were. Will Steffen and colleagues assembled the evidence in 2004 and revised it in 2015 as twenty-four graphs running from 1750 to 2010. Twelve track socio-economic trends including population, real gross domestic product, urban population, primary energy use, fertiliser consumption, large dams, water use, motor vehicles and international tourism. Twelve track earth-system trends including atmospheric carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide, stratospheric ozone, surface temperature, ocean acidification, marine fish capture, coastal nitrogen, tropical forest loss and domesticated land. Nearly all of them bend sharply upward from around 1950. World population roughly tripled between 1950 and 2020; primary energy consumption rose more than fivefold; water withdrawals roughly quadrupled; the number of large dams passed fifty thousand, so heavily regulating the world's rivers that the sediment supply to the Nile and Mississippi deltas collapsed while the land continued to subside.

Underlying much of this was a single chemical process. Nitrogen limits plant growth almost everywhere, and although the atmosphere is seventy-eight percent nitrogen gas, the triple bond in N2 is so strong that almost nothing can break it. Before 1900 agricultural nitrogen came only from legumes, manure and mined guano and nitrate. Fritz Haber demonstrated catalytic ammonia synthesis in 1909 and Carl Bosch scaled it at BASF by 1913, at roughly two hundred atmospheres and 450 degrees Celsius over an iron catalyst. Vaclav Smil has estimated that about half the nitrogen atoms in a living person's proteins passed through the Haber-Bosch process, and that without it the earth would support perhaps four billion people. The unabsorbed remainder leaches as nitrate or escapes as nitrous oxide, a greenhouse gas roughly three hundred times more potent than carbon dioxide per molecule, and feeds algal blooms whose decay strips oxygen from coastal water; the Gulf of Mexico dead zone has repeatedly exceeded fifteen thousand square kilometres.

Synthetic pesticides followed a parallel arc. DDT was found to be insecticidal by Paul Müller in 1939, used to great effect against typhus-carrying lice and malarial mosquitoes, and earned him a Nobel Prize in 1948. Its persistence and fat solubility then produced biomagnification, concentrations rising at each trophic level until peregrines, ospreys and bald eagles laid eggs with shells too thin to survive. Rachel Carson's Silent Spring in 1962 assembled the evidence for a general readership and survived a well-funded campaign against her credibility. The Green Revolution, meanwhile, roughly tripled cereal yields in adopting regions by pairing Norman Borlaug's semi-dwarf wheats with fertiliser, irrigation and pesticides, averting confidently forecast famines while deepening input dependence and eroding crop genetic diversity. The first Earth Day in April 1970 drew perhaps twenty million Americans; the Environmental Protection Agency was created that December, and the United Nations met at Stockholm in 1972.

sections.heading: Climate History and the Reconstruction of Past Weather
sections.body:
Climate history reconstructs past atmospheric conditions and asks how they interacted with human events. It is among the most rapidly advancing parts of the field and among the most methodologically demanding, because the temptation to explain political outcomes by temperature is strong and the evidence rarely supports so direct a link.

The last two millennia contain two well-defined anomalies in the Northern Hemisphere. The Medieval Climate Anomaly, roughly 950 to 1250, was a period of relative warmth in the North Atlantic region that coincided with Norse settlement of Iceland and Greenland and with the European agricultural expansion. The Little Ice Age, conventionally about 1300 to 1850, brought cooler and more variable conditions, with the coldest phases in the seventeenth and early nineteenth centuries. Both were regionally uneven rather than globally synchronous, which is precisely what distinguishes them from modern warming: reconstructions such as the PAGES 2k compilation show no period in the last two thousand years in which more than half the planet experienced its warmest or coldest interval at the same time until the twentieth century.

The mechanisms behind the Little Ice Age are reasonably well understood. Solar output declined during extended sunspot minima, notably the Maunder Minimum from about 1645 to 1715, when observers recorded almost no sunspots for decades. More importantly, several very large volcanic eruptions injected sulphate aerosols into the stratosphere, reflecting sunlight for two to three years each. The 1257 eruption of Samalas in Indonesia was among the largest of the Holocene; the 1600 eruption of Huaynaputina in Peru preceded the Russian famine of 1601 to 1603 that killed perhaps a third of the population; and the 1815 eruption of Tambora, the largest in recorded history, produced the Year Without a Summer in 1816, with snow in New England in June, harvest failure across Europe, and a subsistence crisis that pushed emigration and food riots.

Geoffrey Parker's Global Crisis of 2013 made the most ambitious argument in this area, assembling evidence that the mid-seventeenth century saw simultaneous state breakdown across Eurasia, including the English Civil War, the Fronde in France, the collapse of the Ming dynasty in 1644, and upheaval in the Ottoman and Mughal empires, and connecting these to the coldest phase of the Little Ice Age through harvest failure, fiscal stress and war. Sam White made a comparable case for Ottoman Anatolia. Critics respond, reasonably, that climate stress alone does not determine outcomes, that societies with better granaries, more flexible taxation or less exposed elites weathered identical weather very differently, and that the causal chain runs through institutions at every step. The productive formulation, now broadly accepted, is that climate sets the difficulty of the problem while social arrangements determine whether the problem becomes a catastrophe.

sections.heading: Environmental Justice and the Politics of Exposure
sections.body:
One of the most consequential shifts in the field since the 1980s has been the recognition that environmental harm is distributed according to existing lines of power, and that this distribution is itself a historical process with identifiable decisions behind it. The environmental justice movement in the United States is usually dated to 1982, when residents of predominantly Black Warren County, North Carolina, protested the siting of a landfill for soil contaminated with polychlorinated biphenyls; more than five hundred people were arrested. A 1983 study by the General Accounting Office and a far more influential 1987 report by the United Commission for Racial Justice, Toxic Wastes and Race in the United States, found that race was the strongest predictor of proximity to hazardous waste facilities, stronger than income. Robert Bullard's Dumping in Dixie in 1990 documented the pattern across the American South, and Executive Order 12898 in 1994 formally directed federal agencies to consider such effects.

The insight generalised rapidly. Industrial disasters concentrate their harm on the least protected: the 1984 Union Carbide gas release at Bhopal, which exposed half a million people to methyl isocyanate and killed several thousand immediately and many thousands more over subsequent years, occurred at a plant surrounded by informal settlements with no evacuation planning. Mercury discharged into Minamata Bay by the Chisso Corporation from the 1930s poisoned a fishing community whose complaints were dismissed for decades before methylmercury was confirmed as the cause. Occupational exposure to asbestos, silica, lead and solvents falls on workers rather than on shareholders, and lags in recognition are measured in generations.

Internationally, the same logic appears as unequal ecological exchange: high-income economies import materials and embodied energy while exporting waste and pollution-intensive production. Historians have documented the shipment of hazardous waste and end-of-life ships and electronics to lower-income countries, prompting the Basel Convention of 1989. Joan Martínez-Alier's concept of the environmentalism of the poor names the enormous body of grassroots resistance, from the Chipko forest protests in India to Ken Saro-Wiwa's Ogoni campaign against oil extraction in the Niger Delta, that is motivated by livelihood and survival rather than by wilderness aesthetics, and that has often been invisible to movements organised around the latter.

Parallel to this has come sustained engagement with Indigenous environmental knowledge. Research on Aboriginal Australian fire management, from Rhys Jones's 1969 coining of fire-stick farming to Bill Gammage's detailed reconstruction of a continent shaped by patchwork burning, and comparable work on Californian, Amazonian and North American practices, has established that many landscapes classed as natural were the products of sophisticated long-term management. This has moved from historical claim to policy: cultural burning is now being reintroduced in Australia and North America explicitly to reduce catastrophic fire, which is a rare instance of environmental history directly informing land management.

sections.heading: The Anthropocene Debate
sections.body:
In February 2000, at a meeting in Cuernavaca, the atmospheric chemist Paul Crutzen interrupted repeated references to the Holocene by objecting that the world had left it, and proposed the term Anthropocene. Crutzen and the biologist Eugene Stoermer, who had used the word informally since the 1980s, published the proposal later that year. The claim is geological in form: that human activity has become a stratigraphically significant force, leaving signals in rock and sediment that a future geologist would recognise as marking a new epoch.

Formalising an epoch requires the International Commission on Stratigraphy to accept a Global Boundary Stratotype Section and Point, a physical location where a globally synchronous marker is preserved in sediment. An Anthropocene Working Group was convened in 2009 and worked for over a decade. Candidate start dates were vigorously contested. An early agricultural start, proposed by William Ruddiman, argues that rice paddies and deforestation raised methane and carbon dioxide enough to forestall the next glaciation from about 8,000 and 5,000 years ago respectively. The 1610 Orbis date rests on the carbon dioxide dip following American depopulation. An industrial start around 1780 aligns with fossil fuel use. The date the working group settled on was around 1950, marked by radionuclides from atmospheric nuclear testing, particularly plutonium-239, which appears as an unambiguous global horizon in sediments and ice, accompanied by fly ash, plastics, concrete and elevated nitrogen.

In 2023 the group proposed Crawford Lake in Ontario, a small meromictic lake whose bottom water never mixes and which therefore preserves undisturbed annual layers, as the reference section. In March 2024 the relevant subcommission voted the proposal down. The rejection turned on stratigraphic arguments rather than on any denial that humans are transforming the earth: critics held that a seventy-year interval is too brief to constitute an epoch, that the diachronous and long-running character of human impact suits an event rather than a formal unit, and that the proposal privileged a mid-twentieth-century industrial moment over ten thousand years of agricultural transformation. The term remains in widespread informal use across the sciences and humanities regardless.

For environmental historians the debate has been productive well beyond stratigraphy, because arguing about the start date forces an argument about causation. Naming the epoch after the human species implies that humanity as such is responsible, which sits awkwardly with the fact that emissions and consumption are extraordinarily unequally distributed: the wealthiest ten percent of the world's population accounts for roughly half of consumption-based emissions. Jason Moore proposed Capitalocene to locate the cause in a specific economic system rather than in the species; Donna Haraway offered Plantationocene to foreground the plantation as the template for simplified, coerced landscapes. Each alternative is a compressed historical argument about who did what, and the fact that a term of geological chronology has become a site of political contest is itself a fact about the present.

sections.heading: Persistent Debates, Methodological Traps and the Limits of the Field
sections.body:
Environmental history carries occupational hazards that practitioners name openly, and reading the field well means watching for them. The first is environmental determinism: reducing human outcomes to physical geography or climate. Nineteenth-century versions were explicitly racist, explaining supposed civilisational hierarchies by latitude, and the association has left the field permanently wary. Modern versions are subtler. Jared Diamond's Guns, Germs, and Steel of 1997 argued that Eurasia's east-west axis, its stock of domesticable species and its crowd diseases explain why Europeans conquered rather than the reverse, which many historians found useful at continental scale and unpersuasive at the scale of specific events. His Collapse of 2005 drew sharper criticism, particularly over Rapa Nui, where Terry Hunt and Carl Lipo have argued that introduced rats eating palm seeds and, above all, European contact, disease and Peruvian slave raiding in the 1860s explain the island's fate better than self-inflicted ecocide.

The second trap is declensionism: structuring every narrative as a fall from earlier harmony. It is seductive because it is morally legible and because sources documenting damage outnumber sources documenting stability, but it presumes a stable baseline that often did not exist and can romanticise pre-industrial restraint that reflected limited capacity rather than superior ethics. Recovery stories are real: European forest cover has expanded substantially since 1900, London's air is cleaner than at any time since the seventeenth century, several whale populations have partially rebounded since the 1986 moratorium, and the Montreal Protocol of 1987 put the ozone layer on course to recover by mid-century. A third difficulty is evidential asymmetry: written records are abundant for literate, bureaucratic and recent societies, and physical proxies exist only where lakes, bogs, ice or long-lived trees do, so the map of what is known is uneven for reasons unrelated to where important things happened. A fourth is scale, since a region can gain forest while the global total falls because its timber demand was exported. Daniel Pauly's shifting baseline syndrome, named in 1995, describes how each generation takes the depleted state it inherited as normal, so decline is chronically under-perceived.

Against these limits sit the field's genuine contributions. It supplies the only long-run record of how societies behave under environmental stress, and that record is varied: some innovated past constraints, some exported the burden to colonies and peripheries, some built commons institutions that lasted centuries, and some failed, though almost never for purely environmental reasons and almost never as abruptly as popular accounts suggest. It also supplies calibration. Only historical reconstruction establishes that atmospheric carbon dioxide now exceeds anything in the 800,000-year ice core record, that extinction rates run orders of magnitude above the fossil background, or that North Atlantic cod once supported catches later fishers would find unimaginable. What the field cannot do is predict, because the present differs from every past case, or settle values: showing that wilderness is a cultural construct does not decide whether wild places should be protected. Its most defensible service is removing false premises from those arguments.

guides.title: The Columbian Exchange
guides.summary: The transfer of diseases, crops, animals, people and ideas between the Americas and the rest of the world after 1492, how it reshaped populations and diets on every continent, and what historians still argue about.

sections.heading: What the Columbian Exchange Was
sections.body:
The phrase describes the vast, largely unplanned transfer of living things between the Americas and the rest of the world that began with Christopher Columbus's landfall in the Bahamas on 12 October 1492 and has never really stopped. Diseases, crops, domesticated animals, weeds, insects, people and ideas crossed an ocean that had separated two biological worlds for thousands of years. Within a century the population of the Americas had collapsed by something close to nine-tenths, and within three centuries the staple diets of China, India, Ireland, Italy, west Africa and much of eastern Europe had been rebuilt around plants that did not exist outside the Americas in 1491.

The term was coined by the American historian Alfred W. Crosby in his 1972 book The Columbian Exchange: Biological and Cultural Consequences of 1492. Crosby struggled to place the manuscript; several university presses turned it down, and it eventually appeared from a small commercial publisher. The reason is instructive. Historians of the period wrote about conquistadors, treaties, theology and gold. Crosby proposed that the decisive actors were viruses, bacteria, seeds and hooves, and that European conquest of the Americas was more a biological event than a military one. That idea, uncomfortable at the time, is now close to orthodoxy, and Crosby extended it in 1986 with Ecological Imperialism, which asked why European settlement succeeded so completely in temperate zones such as North America, Argentina, Australia and New Zealand, which he called the neo-Europes, and so poorly in tropical Africa and Asia.

Two features make the exchange historically unique. The first is scale: it was the largest and most abrupt reorganisation of the world's biota since the breakup of the supercontinent Pangaea, compressed into a few human generations rather than geological time. The second is asymmetry. The traffic was not balanced. Lethal epidemic disease flowed overwhelmingly from east to west, while high-calorie, high-yielding crops flowed overwhelmingly from west to east. That asymmetry is the reason the exchange enriched and enlarged Eurasian and African populations while destroying American ones.

It is also worth being precise about what the concept is not. Calling it an exchange can make it sound like a fair trade or an accident of nature, and it was neither. The movement of biota happened inside a structure of invasion, forced labour, enslavement and settlement, and the demographic catastrophe cannot be separated from that structure. Pathogens did the killing, but wars, enslavement in mines, the destruction of food stores, forced resettlement and the collapse of any capacity to nurse the sick multiplied their effect enormously. The most useful way to hold both facts together is to treat the exchange as a biological process that colonial violence loaded, aimed and repeatedly fired.

sections.heading: The World in 1491: Two Separate Biological Experiments
sections.body:
To see why 1492 mattered so much, you have to understand how long the two hemispheres had been apart and how different that made them. Human beings entered the Americas from north-east Asia through Beringia during and after the Last Glacial Maximum, with firm archaeological evidence by around 15,000 years ago and contested evidence for earlier arrivals. Rising sea levels drowned the Bering land bridge roughly 11,000 years ago. From then until 1492, apart from the brief and inconsequential Norse settlement at L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland around the year 1000 and possible Polynesian contact in the eastern Pacific, the two halves of the world exchanged almost nothing.

Both hemispheres then independently invented agriculture, and both did it brilliantly, but with radically different raw material. Old World farmers had wheat, barley, rice, millet, sorghum and rye among the grains, and lentils, peas, chickpeas and soy among the pulses. American farmers domesticated maize from the wild grass teosinte in the Balsas river valley of southern Mexico around 9,000 years ago, potatoes in the high Andes, cassava in Amazonia, and beans, squash, chilli, tomato, cacao, peanut, quinoa and amaranth elsewhere. Neither set overlapped meaningfully with the other.

The truly consequential difference was in animals. Eurasia had cattle, pigs, sheep, goats, horses, donkeys, water buffalo, camels and chickens. Jared Diamond's much-quoted count is that of the fourteen large mammal species domesticated anywhere before the twentieth century, thirteen were Eurasian. The Americas had the llama and alpaca, restricted to the Andes and never used for milk or traction, plus the guinea pig, the turkey and the dog. American societies had no large draught animals north of the Andes, hence no ploughs, no wheeled transport in practical use, and no cavalry.

That animal gap had a second, deadlier consequence. Most human epidemic diseases are zoonoses: they crossed into humans from herd animals living in close, dense, sustained contact with people. Measles is closely related to rinderpest of cattle. Influenza cycles through pigs and waterfowl. Smallpox's nearest known relatives are rodent and camel poxviruses. Tuberculosis, brucellosis and anthrax all have livestock reservoirs. Eurasians spent ten thousand years sharing byres, wells and dung heaps with livestock, dying in enormous numbers as each new pathogen emerged, and the survivors' descendants inherited populations in which these diseases had become endemic childhood illnesses. American populations, lacking the herds, never ran that grim experiment, and therefore carried no acquired immunity to any of it.

None of this means American societies were technologically or intellectually behind. Mesoamerican astronomers tracked Venus with an accuracy Europe would not match for centuries. Inca engineers built roads and suspension bridges across terrain that defeated Spanish carts, administering an empire of millions using the knotted-cord khipu. Tenochtitlan, built on a lake with causeways, aqueducts and chinampa floating gardens, held perhaps 200,000 people when Seville held fewer than 50,000, and Spanish soldiers described it with open astonishment. The asymmetry that mattered in 1492 was not one of civilisation but an accident of which wild species happened to be available for domestication on each landmass.

sections.heading: Why Isolation Made Contact So Lethal
sections.body:
The mechanism behind the American mortality is not mysterious, but it is often explained badly, so it is worth setting out carefully.

Epidemic diseases such as smallpox and measles are what epidemiologists call crowd infections. They confer lasting immunity in survivors, kill or immunise quickly, and cannot persist without a continuous supply of new susceptible hosts. Measles requires a connected population of roughly a quarter of a million people to remain endemic; below that threshold it burns out. In dense Eurasian societies these diseases circulated permanently, infecting children, so that adults were largely immune and remained able to farm, fetch water, nurse and govern even in a bad year.

In the Americas, every one of these pathogens arrived as a novelty into a population of which one hundred per cent were susceptible, regardless of age. That single fact explains most of the difference in outcome. When everybody falls ill in the same fortnight, nobody draws water, nobody nurses the sick, the harvest is not brought in, and the seed corn is eaten. Deaths from dehydration, starvation, exposure and secondary bacterial infection can exceed deaths from the virus itself. Then a second and third disease arrive on a population already weakened and socially shattered.

Historians once explained the catastrophe by innate genetic susceptibility, summed up in the phrase virgin soil epidemics. Two qualifications are now standard. First, low genetic diversity at the human leukocyte antigen loci, which is real in some American populations because of the founder effect of a small migrating group, has never been shown to account for anything like the observed mortality; the evidence for a distinctly American biological fragility is thin. Second, the historian David S. Jones argued influentially in 2003 that leaning on innate susceptibility can quietly excuse the colonists, because it presents the deaths as inevitable rather than as the product of conditions that colonisers created. Warfare, enslavement in mines and on plantations, the destruction of stored food, forced relocation into mission settlements, malnutrition and the deliberate breaking of social structures all raise case fatality dramatically.

The honest formulation is that a completely susceptible population would have suffered terribly under any circumstances, and that the circumstances turned terrible into apocalyptic. Comparable events elsewhere support this. When smallpox reached isolated Pacific and Arctic communities in later centuries under less violent conditions, mortality was severe but generally lower. Where epidemic arrived alongside conquest, as in central Mexico and Peru, it was worse.

One further mechanism explains why the collapse continued rather than ending with a single wave: depopulation is self-reinforcing. Deaths among adults of reproductive age suppress births for a generation. Specialised knowledge held by a few individuals, of irrigation systems, seed stores, medicine or ritual authority, is lost entirely when they die. Political structures fragment, leaving communities open to raiding and enslavement, which spreads the next pathogen further. Each epidemic therefore landed on a society less able to withstand it than the one before, which is why American populations kept falling for a century or more rather than rebounding as Europe did after the Black Death.

sections.heading: The Caribbean Laboratory, 1492 to 1520
sections.body:
The first three decades of contact happened almost entirely in the Caribbean, and everything that followed on the mainland had already been rehearsed there.

Columbus made landfall on an island the Taíno called Guanahaní, which he renamed San Salvador, and went on to establish a foothold on Hispaniola, the island now divided between Haiti and the Dominican Republic. His second voyage in 1493 was a colonising expedition of seventeen ships and some 1,200 men, and its cargo manifest is the true beginning of the exchange: wheat, chickpeas, melons, onions, grape vines, sugar cane cuttings, and horses, cattle, pigs, sheep, goats and chickens.

The Taíno population of Hispaniola at contact is genuinely unknown and fiercely disputed. Bartolomé de las Casas, the Dominican friar who became the fiercest critic of Spanish rule, claimed three million. Modern estimates range from around 60,000 to over a million, with several careful reconstructions near 250,000 to 500,000. What is not disputed is the trajectory. By the census of 1514 the recorded Taíno population of Hispaniola was about 26,000. By the 1540s the Taíno had effectively ceased to exist as an independent society, though genetic and cultural traces persist in Caribbean populations today.

Disease was not the whole story in these first decades. The encomienda system, which granted colonists the labour of specified indigenous communities, drove men into placer gold workings under conditions that killed quickly. Food production collapsed as labour was diverted. Raiding for slaves depopulated the Bahamas and the Lesser Antilles to supply Hispaniola. Suicide, infanticide and refusal to reproduce are reported by several contemporaries, and while such accounts must be read carefully, the demographic effect of shattered family formation is real.

The first unambiguous major epidemic came late, in December 1518 and January 1519, when smallpox reached Hispaniola and killed, by the estimate of the colonial officials themselves, a third to a half of the surviving indigenous population within months. It spread to Puerto Rico and Cuba immediately. Its late arrival is easily explained: the Atlantic crossing took five to eight weeks, longer than the infectious period of smallpox in a small ship's company, so the virus could only cross if it happened to catch a chain of susceptible passengers, or travelled in scabs on cloth.

Two other things were established in these years that would matter for centuries. Sugar cane, brought from the Canaries, was planted on Hispaniola and by the 1510s was being milled; the first enslaved Africans were landed to work it, and the first documented shipment direct from Africa to the Americas sailed in 1518. And the pigs and cattle turned loose to provision future voyages began breeding without predators or competitors, an ecological pattern that would repeat across two continents.

The Caribbean therefore functioned as a rehearsal room. Every institution that would define Spanish and later British America, the encomienda and its successors, the plantation, the mission settlement, the mining draft, the racial hierarchy that sorted people into legal categories, was drafted there on a small population and then exported wholesale to Mexico, Peru and beyond within a single generation.

sections.heading: The Great Dying: Smallpox and the Fall of Empires
sections.body:
From the Caribbean the pathogens moved onto the mainland, and they moved faster than the Europeans did.

Smallpox reached the Valley of Mexico in 1520, carried by the relief expedition under Pánfilo de Narváez sent to arrest Hernán Cortés. Spanish accounts name an infected man in that company, sometimes identified as an enslaved African called Francisco de Eguía, though the sources do not securely establish the individual. The effect is not in doubt. The epidemic struck Tenochtitlan during the siege, killed Cuitláhuac, the Mexica ruler who had just driven the Spanish out on the Noche Triste, and gutted the defending population. Sahagún's indigenous informants described bodies so covered with pustules that the sick could not move, and the starvation that followed because nobody could bring food. Cortés's victory in August 1521 was won over a city that had already lost a large fraction of its people and its leadership.

In the Andes the sequence was starker, because the epidemic arrived before the Europeans did. A disease, most probably smallpox, travelled south through indigenous trade networks and struck the Inca empire around 1524 to 1527, killing the Sapa Inca Huayna Capac and his designated heir within days of each other. The resulting succession war between his sons Huáscar and Atahualpa was still being fought when Francisco Pizarro landed with fewer than two hundred men in 1532.

Smallpox was only the beginning. Measles followed in the 1530s, typhus, influenza and diphtheria after that, and later yellow fever and falciparum malaria in the tropical lowlands. Central Mexico suffered two catastrophic epidemics its Nahua survivors called cocoliztli, in 1545 to 1548 and 1576 to 1580, each killing perhaps a third to a half of the remaining population. A 2018 ancient-DNA study at Teposcolula-Yucundaa in Oaxaca recovered Salmonella enterica serovar Paratyphi C from victims of the 1545 outbreak. That is real evidence, but it identifies a pathogen at one site rather than a proven sole cause; an indigenous viral haemorrhagic fever amplified by drought remains a serious competing hypothesis. The pattern held for three centuries, reaching the Pacific Northwest in the 1770s and the northern plains most notoriously in 1837, when smallpox carried up the Missouri by steamboat destroyed much of the Mandan, Hidatsa and Arikara.

Two clarifications matter for reading this history accurately. The first is that these epidemics repeatedly outran the Europeans themselves, moving along indigenous trade and diplomatic networks far more extensive than colonists understood. Many communities in the North American interior and in Amazonia were devastated years or decades before they met a European, which is one reason later arrivals found what looked like thinly settled wilderness and concluded it had always been so. The second is that deliberate infection, though it looms large in popular memory, was rare. The best-documented case is the 1763 correspondence of Sir Jeffery Amherst and Colonel Henry Bouquet at Fort Pitt, discussing distributing smallpox-infected blankets to besieging Native forces. Such episodes are real and damning, but they are not what killed tens of millions; the ordinary machinery of contact and conquest did that without needing intent.

sections.heading: Counting the Dead: Estimates and Their Uncertainty
sections.body:
How many people lived in the Americas in 1491 is one of the most contested numbers in history, and any account that gives a single confident figure should be treated with suspicion.

The estimates have swung wildly. In the 1930s and 1940s the anthropologist Alfred Kroeber put the total for the hemisphere at around 8.4 million, a figure now regarded as far too low and shaped by the assumption that the sparse populations observed by nineteenth-century ethnographers reflected pre-contact conditions. In 1966 Henry Dobyns, working backward from depopulation ratios, proposed 90 to 112 million. The methods behind that high figure, essentially multiplying a nadir population by an assumed mortality rate, have been heavily criticised for circularity.

Modern work has converged on an intermediate range. William Denevan's synthesis in The Native Population of the Americas in 1492 gave about 54 million. A 2019 study by Alexander Koch and colleagues at University College London, which aggregated regional estimates, arrived at roughly 60.5 million, with an uncertainty range of about 45 to 80 million. Central Mexico alone probably held between 10 and 25 million, the Andes perhaps 9 to 12 million, Amazonia several million more than was long assumed, and North America north of Mexico something in the range of 2 to 7 million.

The nadir is easier to establish because colonial administrations counted taxpayers. Across the hemisphere the indigenous population bottomed out around 1600 to 1650 at roughly 5 to 6 million. That implies a decline of about ninety per cent, which is why the period is often called the Great Dying. For comparison, the Black Death killed perhaps thirty to sixty per cent of Europe over roughly seven years; the American collapse was deeper, though spread over a longer period and driven by many diseases rather than one.

The sources of uncertainty are worth naming, because they explain why the debate persists. Pre-contact societies left no censuses, so estimates rest on archaeological settlement counts, carrying-capacity models based on agricultural systems, early colonial tribute lists that counted only taxable adult men in conquered areas, and back-projection from later counts. Each method has systematic biases in a different direction. Colonial tribute lists undercount the unconquered and the fleeing. Carrying-capacity models depend on assumptions about diet and land use that are themselves inferred. And the epidemics that most interest us frequently preceded the record-keepers, so the first written count of many regions was already a count of survivors.

The politics are unavoidable and should be acknowledged. Higher pre-contact figures imply a larger catastrophe and a more sophisticated indigenous world; lower figures have historically been used to portray the Americas as empty and available. Good scholarship on both sides exists, but the numbers have never been politically neutral.

sections.heading: Maize and the Potato: Two Plants That Rebuilt the Old World
sections.body:
If disease is the exchange's tragedy, American staple crops are its enormous, largely unacknowledged demographic gift to everyone else. Four of the world's most important food plants, maize, potato, cassava and sweet potato, are American. Together they now supply a substantial share of humanity's calories, and every one of those calories was unavailable outside the Americas before 1492.

Maize is the more travelled. Domesticated from teosinte in southern Mexico around 9,000 years ago and bred into thousands of landraces, it reached Spain within a few years of Columbus and spread with astonishing speed along Ottoman, Portuguese and Arab trade routes. It was being grown in the Balkans, Egypt and west Africa within decades; Chinese local gazetteers record it by the middle of the sixteenth century. Its advantages are structural. Maize yields more calories per hectare than wheat on many soils, tolerates a wider range of conditions, matures quickly enough to fit between other crops, and produces both grain and fodder. In parts of Africa it displaced sorghum and millet so thoroughly that it is now assumed to be indigenous.

Maize also carried a hidden defect that Europe learned the hard way. The niacin in maize is chemically bound and largely unavailable to human digestion. Mesoamerican cooks had solved this thousands of years earlier by nixtamalisation, soaking the grain in an alkaline solution of wood ash or slaked lime, which frees the niacin and improves protein quality. Europe imported the grain and not the technique. The result was pellagra, a deficiency disease of dermatitis, diarrhoea and dementia that killed tens of thousands in northern Italy, Spain, Romania and, well into the twentieth century, the American South, where Joseph Goldberger established its dietary cause in the 1910s against fierce resistance from those who insisted it was infectious.

The potato had a slower start and a bigger long-run effect on Europe. Domesticated in the Andes between 8,000 and 10,000 years ago in bewildering genetic variety, it reached Spain around 1570 and was treated for two centuries as a curiosity, a famine food or animal fodder, partly because it belongs to the nightshade family and partly because Europeans distrusted a plant grown from tubers rather than seed. Its adoption was driven by war and by advocacy: Frederick the Great ordered planting in Prussia from 1756, and Antoine-Augustin Parmentier campaigned for it in France after surviving on potatoes as a prisoner of war. The economists Nathan Nunn and Nancy Qian estimated in 2011 that the potato accounts for roughly a quarter of the growth in Old World population and urbanisation between 1700 and 1900, an extraordinary claim for a single crop, and one built on comparing regions by their suitability for potato cultivation before and after introduction.

sections.heading: Cassava, Chilli, Tomato and the Rest of the American Cargo
sections.body:
Beyond the two great staples, the list of American plants that reshaped other continents is long enough that most cuisines now considered traditional would be unrecognisable without them.

Cassava, also called manioc or yuca, was domesticated in Amazonia and carried by Portuguese traders from Brazil to west and central Africa in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. It is drought-tolerant, thrives on poor acidic soils, can be left in the ground for months as a living store, and yields more calories per hectare than almost any other crop. It now feeds several hundred million people across Africa and is the continent's second most important source of calories. It carries its own hazard: bitter varieties contain cyanogenic glycosides that release hydrogen cyanide, and the elaborate American processing techniques of grating, pressing, soaking and roasting travelled with it only partially. Inadequate processing still causes cyanide poisoning and the irreversible paralytic disease konzo in parts of central Africa during food shortages.

The sweet potato, unrelated to the potato despite the name, reached China in the 1590s, traditionally credited to the Fujian merchant Chen Zhenlong who is said to have smuggled cuttings from the Philippines. It grew on hillsides and sandy soils useless for rice, and became a survival crop of the poor across southern China. The historian Ho Ping-ti argued that American crops underwrote the extraordinary Chinese population growth from roughly 150 million in 1700 to over 400 million by 1850. Later scholarship has qualified this, noting that most of the increase came from intensified rice cultivation and that maize and sweet potato mattered most at the frontier and on marginal upland, where their cultivation also caused serious erosion.

Chilli peppers, domesticated in Mexico and Bolivia, spread through Portuguese networks to India, south-east Asia, Korea and west Africa within a century, and are now so central to those cuisines that their arrival date surprises people. Tomatoes reached Europe in the 1540s and were regarded with suspicion for two hundred years before becoming inseparable from Italian cooking in the nineteenth century. Cacao, vanilla, peanuts, pineapple, avocado, pumpkins and squashes, common beans, sunflowers, papaya and the turkey all made the same journey.

Three American plants changed history for reasons other than food. Tobacco became the first mass consumer commodity of the Atlantic world, financing the Virginia colony after 1612 and later killing on a scale that dwarfs any epidemic in this account. Cinchona bark from the eastern Andes, the source of quinine, made it possible for Europeans to survive long enough in malarial Africa and Asia to conquer them, which is to say that an American tree was a necessary condition for nineteenth-century European imperialism elsewhere. And the rubber tree, Hevea brasiliensis, tapped in Amazonia and later transplanted to British Malaya from seed collected in 1876, supplied the material without which no vehicle of the industrial age would roll.

sections.heading: Wheat, Sugar, Coffee and Rice Go West
sections.body:
The eastward flow of crops was more spectacular in its consequences, but the westward flow reorganised American landscapes just as thoroughly, and it was more deliberate. Colonists wanted to eat what they had eaten at home, and they planted accordingly.

Wheat came first and struggled. It did poorly in the tropical Caribbean and in humid lowlands, but it took hold in the highlands of Mexico, in Chile and Argentina, and eventually across the North American plains, where by the late nineteenth century it would grow on a scale that collapsed grain prices in Europe. Barley, rye, oats, lentils, cabbages, turnips, olives, grapes and citrus followed the same pattern of experiment and regional success.

Sugar cane was the transformative one. Domesticated in New Guinea and refined into an industry by medieval Arab and then Iberian planters, it had already been developed as a plantation monoculture on Madeira, the Canaries and São Tomé, complete with enslaved African labour, before it reached the Americas. Columbus carried cuttings on his second voyage. From Hispaniola it moved to Brazil, where Pernambuco and Bahia dominated world production for a century, and then to Barbados, whose sugar revolution in the 1640s created the model Jamaica and Saint-Domingue would industrialise. Sugar built the Atlantic slave system, because it demanded enormous coordinated labour at harvest and milling within hours of cutting.

Coffee, a plant of the Ethiopian highlands cultivated commercially in Yemen, reached Martinique in the 1720s; from a handful of plants it became the basis of the Brazilian and Colombian economies. Bananas and plantains, originally from south-east Asia by way of Africa, became staple foods across the American tropics. Rice arrived by two routes, Asian rice through Europe and African rice with enslaved west Africans, and the expertise of enslaved growers from the Senegambia and the Rice Coast was decisive in establishing the tidal rice plantations of South Carolina and Georgia, a case where the exchange transferred not just a plant but a body of technical knowledge held by the enslaved.
